# Introduction

## Background and Motivation

Cluster randomized trials (CRTs) randomize intact groups, such as clinics, schools, or geographic areas, rather than individuals. They are the standard design when an intervention is delivered at the group level or when individual randomization would create unacceptable contamination between arms [@donner_design_2000; @hayes_cluster_2017]. Standard CRT analysis relies on the no-interference component of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): a cluster's outcome must not depend on which other clusters were assigned to treatment [@Rubin1986]. This assumption comes from the theory of individually randomized trials. It can fail once clusters are spatially arranged, as can the weaker assumption of partial interference, under which outcomes may depend on assignments within prespecified groups but not across them [@hudgens_toward_2008]. Tobler's first law of geography states that "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" [@tobler_computer_1970]. By this principle, an intervention delivered in one location can plausibly influence outcomes in adjacent locations through shared populations, service networks, information diffusion, or environmental pathways. Documented examples of spatial spillover come from public health and development economics. In a trial of insecticide-treated bed nets in northern Ghana, children who did not use the nets had lower mortality the closer they lived to a compound with treated nets [@binka_impact_1998]. A school-based deworming trial in Kenya found health and attendance benefits among untreated children near treated schools [@miguel_worms_2004]. When control clusters benefit from nearby treatment, an unadjusted comparison of treated and control clusters may understate the direct effect [@baird_optimal_2018; @leung_rateoptimal_2022]. How much contamination occurs can depend on the spatial arrangement of the two arms, not only on the number of clusters allocated to each [@walther_spatial_2026].

Methods for spatial interference in CRTs have concentrated on correction at the analysis stage. Spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's $I$ [@moran_notes_1950] detect residual spatial dependence once outcomes have been observed. Spatial regression models, such as the spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009] estimated by maximum likelihood [@ord_estimation_1975] and implemented in software [@bivand_r_2022], allow an analyst to separate a direct treatment effect from a spillover effect after the fact. Jarvis and colleagues' systematic review of spatial analysis methods in cluster randomized trials excluded studies that dealt with spatial effects only at the design stage, for example with buffer zones or well-separated clusters [@jarvis_spatial_2017]. Therefore, the literature offers much more guidance on analyzing spatial effects than on how the choice of treatment assignment itself, made before any data are collected, might reduce the problem.

Design-stage tools do exist, but they were largely developed for a different purpose. Restricted and covariate-constrained randomization address the baseline imbalance that a limited number of clusters can produce [@raab_balance_2001; @moulton_covariatebased_2004]. Crisp and colleagues noted that their extension, which selects clusters from a larger eligible set, also increases spatial dispersion among the selected clusters [@crisp_covariate-constrained_2023]. Their dispersion criterion concerns which clusters are selected, not how they are assigned to arms. Balancing a covariate across arms also does not by itself determine whether treated and control clusters are spatially interspersed in a way that induces contamination. Other work addresses the problem studied here more directly. Randomized saturation designs assign different fractions of units treated to different groups so that direct and spillover effects can be jointly identified [@baird_optimal_2018]. Another approach selects whole clusters for inclusion or exclusion in place of a "fried-egg" design that omits each cluster's outer area from analysis [@mccann_spatial_2018]. Recent theoretical work develops designs under spatial, network and cross-cluster interference and spatio-temporal heterogeneity [@leung_rateoptimal_2022; @cai_independentset_2023; @leung_clusterrandomized_2025; @watson_design_2025]. This chapter complements that work with a simulation comparison of concrete assignment designs that a trial team could implement.

Chapter 2 addressed the design stage. It compared simple random sampling (SRS) with Block Stratified Sampling (BSS), which alternates treated and control clusters so that, wherever the two arms can be the same size, no two clusters that share an edge are in the same arm. Its grids had 8 to 12 clusters. It judged each design by its average estimation error and by the risk that a trial's single realized allocation, its treatment assignment, gives a poor estimate. Every cluster in that comparison had the same baseline risk. In many trials incidence varies across the study region. Sudden unexpected death (SUD) in North Carolina (NC) is one example, with higher incidence in rural than in urban counties [@gan_factors_2019]. A trial team that knows historical incidence may want to use it when assigning treatment, to balance incidence across arms, to vary the share of clusters treated by region or to direct treatment toward high-incidence areas. These goals need not lead to the same allocation. We are not aware of a study that compares incidence-informed allocation designs when spillover and spatial dependence are both present. This chapter extends Chapter 2 to that setting, with more designs, a larger grid and heterogeneous incidence. As a result, its results are not a direct numerical replication of Chapter 2.

## Aims and Contributions

This chapter has three aims. The first is to compare treatment assignment designs for a spatial CRT by mean squared error (MSE), bias and confidence interval coverage when incidence is heterogeneous. The second is to assess how those conclusions depend on the incidence pattern, spatial dependence, the spillover regime and the size of the treatment effect. The third is a case study, a simulation based on observed North Carolina incidence, that assesses both average accuracy and the risk of a poor allocation and recommends a design for a statewide extension of a SUD-prevention education pilot trial.

The first contribution is a simulation comparison, on a 100-cluster grid, of eight assignment designs that use geographic restrictions, incidence or both, with SRS as the benchmark. Six are compared in detail, and the appendix documents two related variants. One of the eight, Checkerboard, is Chapter 2's BSS design under another name, and we use the name Checkerboard throughout this chapter. The others include incidence balancing, incidence targeting, saturation and isolation designs. The grid study varied the mechanism that generated incidence, the strength of spatial dependence and the magnitude of spillover. It also varied whether spillover reached only control clusters or both arms, and the treatment effect, with queen contiguity as the primary neighbor definition and rook contiguity as a sensitivity analysis. We analyzed every design with a spatial lag model that includes the spillover term, and a second sensitivity analysis omitted that term. We judged each design by its bias, interval coverage, average MSE and the MSE of its worst allocations.

The second contribution is a case study on the community college service areas of North Carolina, using observed SUD incidence for each planning year. It evaluated the same designs, adapted to an irregular geography, and estimated power and the number of colleges needed when only some colleges take part, with sensitivity analyses of the outcome model and spatial structure. The case study takes observed incidence and geography as fixed inputs and simulates a continuous education outcome. It does not assume that historical SUD incidence predicts education performance, and it does not report outcomes from an implemented intervention. Together, these results indicate which designs to prefer when spillover is expected to reach only control clusters and when it is expected to reach both arms.

The rest of the chapter is organized as follows. @sec-methods sets out the spatial weights and outcome model, the incidence surfaces, the treatment assignment designs, the estimator and performance criteria, and the grid simulation. @sec-results compares the designs on the grid under queen contiguity, by spillover regime and against SRS, then across incidence configurations and parameter settings, treatment effect sizes and individual allocations. @sec-application presents the North Carolina case study, including participation and power. @sec-discussion summarizes the findings, gives design guidance by spillover regime, states the limitations and describes future work. The appendix gives the simulation mechanics, identification and technical notes, the case-study methods, the comparison of all candidate designs and supplementary results, including the sensitivity analyses for rook contiguity and for a model without the spillover term.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Spatial Weights and Outcome Model

The grid study uses a $10\times10$ regular grid of 100 clusters, and the case study uses 58 community college service areas in North Carolina. In both, clusters are linked by a row-standardized spatial weights matrix $\mathbf{W}$ with elements $w_{ij} = 1/d_i$ when clusters $i$ and $j$ are neighbors and $w_{ij} = 0$ otherwise, where $d_i$ is the number of neighbors of cluster $i$. For a treatment assignment vector $\mathbf{Z}$, the element $(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z})_i$ is then the proportion of cluster $i$'s neighbors that are treated, and $(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Y})_i$ is the average outcome among its neighbors. Row-standardization expresses each cluster's spillover exposure as an average over its own neighborhood rather than a raw sum, which would otherwise depend on how many neighbors the cluster has. Within a scenario, the same neighbor definition (@sec-simulation) defines $\mathbf{W}$ in the outcome model, in the Isolation Buffer design, and in the fitted model.

Cluster-level outcomes $\mathbf{Y}$ were generated from a spatial lag model with a spillover term [@ord_estimation_1975],
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{Y} = (\mathbf{I} - \rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}\left[\beta \mathbf{Z} + \psi\,\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) + \tau \mathbf{X} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\right],
\label{eq:outcome}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{Z} \in \{0,1\}^{N}$ is the treatment assignment of the $N$ clusters produced by the design under evaluation, $\beta$ is the direct treatment effect of interest, $\psi$ is the spillover magnitude, $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z})$ is the spillover covariate defined in Equation \ref{eq:spillover}, $\rho$ is the spatial autoregressive coefficient governing dependence in the outcome beyond that induced by treatment and spillover, $\mathbf{X}$ is cluster-level incidence with coefficient $\tau$, and $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is independent standard normal noise ($\sigma = 1$). Therefore, the intervention effect $\beta$ is in units of the noise standard deviation. The spatial multiplier $(\mathbf{I}-\rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}$ spreads each cluster's random error to its neighbors, and from them to their neighbors. The effect $\beta$ is the coefficient of a cluster's own treatment before spatial propagation, not an average total effect after applying $(\mathbf{I}-\rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}$. When $\rho = 0$ the multiplier is the identity and the model is a linear regression with independent errors, $\mathbf{Y} = \beta \mathbf{Z} + \psi\,\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) + \tau \mathbf{X} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$, in which spatial structure enters only through the spillover term. Larger values of $\rho$ induce progressively stronger spatial clustering in the outcome. The incidence coefficient $\tau$ sets how strongly cluster-level incidence shifts the outcome, holding treatment and spillover fixed. With $\tau = 0$, incidence guides only the allocation, as in the case study. With $\tau > 0$, clusters with higher incidence have higher outcomes, as on the grid. Its values and the reason for them are given in @sec-simulation.

This notation follows Chapter 2: $\beta$ is the intervention effect, $\psi$ the spillover magnitude and $\rho$ the spatial dependence coefficient. Chapter 2's treatment indicator $x$ and spillover exposure $z$ correspond here to $\mathbf{Z}$ and $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z})$, and $\mathbf{X}$ here denotes incidence.

We evaluated two spillover regimes,
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z} \quad \text{(both arms)}, \qquad \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z} \circ (\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}) \quad \text{(control only)},
\label{eq:spillover}
\end{equation}
where $\circ$ denotes the elementwise product, which multiplies the two vectors cluster by cluster. The share of treated neighbors $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z}$ is an exposure mapping, a function that assigns each cluster an exposure from the full assignment vector [@aronow_estimating_2017; @forastiere_identification_2021]. Under the control-only regime, only untreated clusters respond to the treatment status of their neighbors. This is classical contamination: an untreated cluster's outcome rises with the share of its neighbors that are treated. Under the both-arms regime, every cluster responds to its neighbors' treatment regardless of its own assignment. Therefore, neighboring treatment adds to a treated cluster's own effect. Chapter 2 used a binary indicator of any treated neighbor in place of the proportion of treated neighbors. The case study compares the binary, count and proportional forms (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}).

## Incidence Surfaces {#sec-incidence}

Chapter 2 assumed that every cluster had the same outcome risk. Cluster-level health outcomes typically vary across space, and the designs studied here differ in whether and how they use that variation. The grid study uses simulated incidence, and the North Carolina data enter only the case study (@sec-application). An incidence configuration is a generating model for $\mathbf{X}$ together with its spatial dependence $\rho_X$, and an incidence surface is one draw of $\mathbf{X}$ over the grid. We generated $\mathbf{X}$, with values in $(0, 1)$, under three mechanisms. Under the independent and identically distributed (iid) mechanism, each $X_i$ is drawn from a Uniform$(0,1)$ distribution, with no spatial structure. The spatially autocorrelated mechanism sets $\mathbf{X} = \Phi\{(\mathbf{I} - \rho_X \mathbf{W}_Q)^{-1} \mathbf{u}\}$, where $\mathbf{u} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function applied elementwise, $\mathbf{W}_Q$ is the queen weights matrix, and $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$. Under the Poisson mechanism, a spatially autocorrelated log-rate surface, $\log \boldsymbol{\lambda} = \log(35/100{,}000) + (\mathbf{I} - \rho_X \mathbf{W}_Q)^{-1} \mathbf{u}$ with $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$, generates cluster death counts $C_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i P)$, with an equal population of $P = 100{,}000$ in every cluster, which means a cluster at the base rate expects 35 deaths. The observed rates $C_i / P$ are then rank-normalized to $X_i = (r_i - 0.5)/N$, where $r_i$ is the rank of cluster $i$'s rate among the $N = 100$ clusters and tied rates share their average rank. Ties remain at this population size: the Poisson surfaces used here have between 60 and 76 distinct values among the 100 clusters.

The base rate of 35 per 100,000 was chosen to represent published SUD incidence. It lies between the SUD incidence rates that Mirzaei and colleagues estimated for US men (49.3 per 100,000) and women (21.7 per 100,000) aged 20--64, close to their average [@mirzaei_years_2019]. It is not the observed rate of the county data described in @sec-application, which come from a different source, age range, period, and case definition. The incidence surfaces are identical under rook and queen contiguity, since the incidence filters always use the queen weights $\mathbf{W}_Q$, whichever neighbor type the scenario uses.

The iid mechanism and the two strengths of each of the other two mechanisms give five incidence configurations. Every mechanism puts incidence on the $(0, 1)$ scale. Therefore, one value of $\tau$ sets the same outcome shift between the lowest and highest possible incidence in every configuration, although the spread of incidence between those limits differs somewhat by mechanism. Comparing the five configurations tests whether the ranking of designs depends on whether incidence is spatially structured and on whether it comes from counts with ties. None of them changed the ranking (@sec-config).

For each configuration we generated $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_{10}$, each from its own seed. The same ten surfaces were used by every scenario in that configuration, across neighbor types, outcome-model parameters, designs, and values of $\beta$. The design draws and the outcome noise are shared more selectively, as described in @sec-simulation. We applied each design to the surface that generated the outcome: assignments for surface $k$ were drawn from $\mathbf{X}_k$, and the outcome and the fitted model for those assignments used $\mathbf{X}_k$ as well. We call this the matched-surface assumption: the incidence observed when a trial is planned is the incidence that drives its outcome. The target of each scenario is performance averaged over incidence surfaces. For example, $\text{MSE} = E_{\mathbf{X}} E_{\mathbf{Z} \mid \mathbf{X}} E_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}[(\hat\beta - \beta)^2]$, with $\mathbf{X}$ drawn from the configuration's generator, $\mathbf{Z}$ from the design given $\mathbf{X}$, and $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. Bias, coverage, and power are defined in the same way.

## Treatment Assignment Designs {#sec-designs}

We implemented eight treatment assignment designs and present six of them as the primary comparison set in this chapter. The other two, Saturation Quadrants and Balanced Halves, are variants of Incidence-Guided Saturation and Balanced Quartiles that could not be distinguished from them under either neighbor type. Appendix \ref{app:eight-design} describes both and gives the comparison of all eight designs with SRS.

Table \ref{tab:designs} describes the six retained designs, and Figure \ref{fig:design-samples} shows one assignment from each, and from SRS, on a single illustrative incidence surface. Checkerboard is the only deterministic design: it gives the same assignment in every draw, although each of its fits still receives its own outcome noise. Every other design was drawn independently 25 times for each incidence surface. Designs that rank clusters by incidence break ties at random, separately for each draw. High Incidence Focus is random only through that tie-breaking. Under the iid and spatial mechanisms, incidence values are distinct, which means High Incidence Focus gives the same assignment in all 25 draws on a surface, and that assignment changes only from one surface to the next. Isolation Buffer builds its assignment from the neighbor type of the scenario, and it treats 38 clusters on average under rook contiguity and 21 under queen contiguity. Every other design treats exactly 50.

## Estimation and Performance Criteria {#sec-estimation}

We estimated $\beta$ with two maximum likelihood spatial lag models, both fit to every simulated outcome and both including an intercept. The primary, oracle model has the spatial lag $\rho \mathbf{W}\mathbf{Y}$ and the covariates $\mathbf{Z}$, $\text{Spill} = \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z})$, and $\mathbf{X}_k$, which matches the outcome model in Equation \ref{eq:outcome}, including the true regime-specific spillover covariate from Equation \ref{eq:spillover}. The oracle model assumes that the analyst knows the form of the spillover mechanism and has the exact exposure term. Therefore, its results are a best case for each design. We return to this assumption as a limitation. The non-oracle model, a sensitivity analysis, has the covariates $\mathbf{Z}$ and $\mathbf{X}_k$ only and omits the spillover term. Both models are fit to the same outcomes.

We fit both models with our own implementation of the maximum likelihood estimator of the spatial lag model [@bivand_comparing_2015], the same estimator that the `lagsarlm` function of the R package `spatialreg` computes with `method = "eigen"`. It maximizes the concentrated log-likelihood over $\rho$, computing the log-determinant from the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{W}$ [@ord_estimation_1975], estimates the remaining coefficients by least squares given $\hat\rho$, and computes standard errors from the analytic information matrix. On 5,120 validation fits it agreed with `lagsarlm` to within $9.7\times10^{-8}$ in $\hat\beta$ and to a relative difference of $1.1\times10^{-8}$ in its standard error, at roughly 1\% of the computing time. We report 95\% confidence intervals $\hat\beta \pm q\,\widehat{\text{SE}}\sqrt{N/(N-p)}$, where $\widehat{\text{SE}}$ is the estimated standard error, $N = 100$ is the number of clusters, and $q = t_{0.975,\,N-p}$. Here $p$ is the number of regression coefficients plus $\rho$, which is 5 for the oracle model and 4 for the non-oracle model and for rook Checkerboard, whose aliased spillover column is dropped. The factor $\sqrt{N/(N-p)}$ replaces the maximum likelihood variance divisor $N$ with $N-p$, the divisor of the unbiased residual variance in linear regression and of the HC1 covariance estimator [@mackinnon_heteroskedasticity_1985]. In the spatial lag model this rescaling is approximate, and we adopted it because it gave nominal coverage in calibration runs (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}). The $t$ quantile allows for the small number of clusters [@leyrat_cluster_2018]. The 95\% Wald interval [@lee_asymptotic_2004] uses $q = z_{0.975} = 1.96$ without the factor, and it covered about one percentage point less for every design (Table \ref{tab:interval-comparison}). The case study uses the same interval with $N = 58$ and $p = 4$, or 54 degrees of freedom, and $p = 5$ in the sensitivity analysis that adds incidence to the fitted model.

For Checkerboard, strict interspersion makes treatment and spillover hard or impossible to separate. Under rook contiguity on the rectangular grid, $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{Z}$, which means treatment and spillover cannot be separated. The parameter $\beta$ is then not identifiable, and the fitted coefficient on treatment estimates $\beta-\psi$. Under queen contiguity, treatment is identifiable but control-only spillover is weakly separated from treatment. We retain Checkerboard in the main design comparison and flag aliased estimates. Exact matrix identities, boundary information and the rare Isolation Buffer aliases are detailed in Appendix \ref{app:technical}. These diagnostics apply only to the two models fit here.

A trial draws only one allocation. Therefore, we judge each design on two criteria, the error of the estimate averaged over the allocations the design can produce and how that error varies from one allocation to another. For the second, we asked how large the MSE can be for a particular assignment. The risk of assignment $a$ is the conditional MSE $m(a)=E_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}[(\hat\beta-\beta)^2\mid a,\mathbf{X}]$, the expected squared error of the estimate if $a$ were the assignment realized. We estimated it by simulating repeated outcomes for each sampled assignment and then compared its distribution across assignments. This distribution across assignments differs from the distribution of squared errors in a single allocation and from MSE across parameter scenarios.

A design's MSE is the average of $m(a)$ over its assignments and, in the grid study, over incidence surfaces. Bias, coverage of the 95\% interval and power are averaged over assignments and outcome noise in the same way. We summarize the variation across assignments by the estimated 90th percentile of $m(a)$ among sampled assignments and by the worst-decile mean, the mean of $m(a)$ over the worst 10\% of sampled assignments.

## Simulation Design {#sec-simulation}

Clusters are neighbors under queen contiguity if they share an edge or a corner, and under rook contiguity if they share an edge [@bivand_applied_2008]. Queen contiguity is the primary analysis in this chapter. Rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis and the case that continues Chapter 2, whose grids used rook neighbors.

We tested four values of the outcome spatial dependence, $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$, four spillover magnitudes, $\psi \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, and five magnitudes of the direct effect, $\beta \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$, with $\beta = 1$ as the primary scenario throughout. The full simulation crossed five values of $\beta$, five incidence configurations, two neighbor types, four values of $\rho$, four values of $\psi$, two spillover regimes, and eight designs, for $5 \times 5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 8 = 12{,}800$ scenarios, of which the six designs reported in this chapter account for 9,600. We call a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\psi$, and spillover regime a block. This gives $5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 = 320$ blocks, 160 for each neighbor type. At the primary scenario, $\beta = 1$, the six designs give 1,920 scenarios, and every block contains all six.

The investigator specifies $\tau$ according to whether incidence is expected to shift the outcome. It is not estimated at the design stage, and we set $\tau = 1$ in the grid simulation. Incidence ranges from 0 to 1, and $\tau = 1$ raises the outcome by one noise standard deviation from the lowest to the highest incidence before spatial spread. That shift equals the primary intervention effect $\beta = 1$. With incidence shifting the outcome, a design whose treatment follows incidence is partly confounded with it, which is the harder case for designs that use incidence. The value may need adjusting for a particular outcome, and estimating it from trial data is left for future work. The case study uses $\tau = 0$ for its education outcome, which is not expected to depend on SUD incidence, and $\tau = 1$ as a hypothetical sensitivity analysis.

Within each scenario, we drew $J = 25$ assignments from each of the $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, for 250 fits per scenario. Every fit had its own noise vector, and fit $(k, j)$ has outcome $\mathbf{Y}_{kj} = (\mathbf{I} - \rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}[\beta \mathbf{Z}_{kj} + \psi\,\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}_{kj}) + \tau \mathbf{X}_k + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{kj}]$. Checkerboard's 250 fits share one assignment but have 250 distinct noise vectors. The ten surfaces are independent, which makes the surface the primary sampling unit. Each estimator was fit 3.2 million times. SRS assigns exactly 50 of the 100 clusters to treatment by complete randomization, ignoring incidence and geography. We ran it afterward with the same matched surfaces, noise keys and 250-fit structure, which brought the complete benchmark to 14,400 scenarios and 3.6 million fits per estimator. Adding SRS left the original eight-design results unchanged.

Every random draw was seeded from a key that names the draw, which makes the results independent of run order and gives common random numbers (Appendix \ref{app:mechanics}). Within a block, all designs share the same noise vectors and incidence surfaces, the five values of $\beta$ reuse the same assignments and noise, and the oracle and non-oracle models are fit to the same outcomes. Blocks within an incidence configuration share its ten surfaces.

For each scenario and estimator, we computed bias, the standard deviation (SD) of $\hat\beta$, MSE, coverage of the 95\% $t$-based interval, and power, the fraction of fits whose $t$-based interval lies above zero (a one-sided test of $\beta = 0$ at level 0.025). For both estimators, every one of the 250 fits in every scenario was valid, with a finite estimate and standard error, and the fitting routine raised no warning other than the aliasing flags described above. Each metric is estimated from a finite number of simulated datasets. Therefore, it carries Monte Carlo error. Its Monte Carlo standard error measures this uncertainty and shrinks as more datasets are simulated [@morris_using_2019]. Monte Carlo standard errors come from the surface-level metrics: with $u_k$ a metric computed on the 25 fits from surface $k$, $\text{SE}(u) = \text{sd}(u_1, \dots, u_{10})/\sqrt{10}$, and, for metrics pooled over the five incidence configurations, from the 50 independent configuration-by-surface means. Appendix \ref{app:mechanics} gives the parameter grid, the seed keys, and the exact formulas for the metrics, their standard errors, and paired differences between designs.

We compared designs with Friedman rank-sum tests over the 160 blocks of each neighbor type, followed at $\beta = 1$ by Nemenyi and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon comparisons, and with paired Wilcoxon tests over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units, which do not treat blocks that share surfaces as independent (Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons}).

We also ran an allocation-risk study with queen weights, $\beta=1$, all ten surfaces from each incidence configuration and the extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\psi$, $\rho\in\{0,0.5\}$ and $\psi\in\{0.5,0.8\}$. The study used 100 assignment draws for each randomized design and 100 simulated outcomes per distinct assignment. As a precision check, one setting (surface 1, $\rho=0.5$, $\psi=0.8$) was refined to 400 outcomes on the same assignments. A design with only one possible assignment received its own outcome replication.

We report results separately for each neighbor type, with queen contiguity primary, and never average a number over the two. Unless stated otherwise, every number in the Results is pooled over the five incidence configurations, and every table and figure caption states whether it pools the configurations or shows them separately. We report the ranking within each configuration separately and show the split wherever a conclusion changes.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Design Performance Under Queen Contiguity {#sec-queen}

At the primary scenario, $\beta = 1$, under queen contiguity and pooled over the five incidence configurations, Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest mean squared error (MSE = 0.091), followed by Balanced Quartiles (0.131), Isolation Buffer (0.160), High Incidence Focus (0.245), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.319), and Checkerboard (1.087) (Table \ref{tab:performance}, Figure \ref{fig:mse}). Coverage of the 95\% $t$-based intervals was between 0.946 and 0.950 for all six designs. Power to reject $\beta = 0$ (one-sided, level 0.025) was 0.921 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, 0.814 for Balanced Quartiles, 0.706 for Isolation Buffer, 0.629 for $2\times2$ Blocking, 0.582 for High Incidence Focus, and 0.538 for Checkerboard.

The Friedman test rejected equal MSE ranks across the six designs and SRS ($\chi^2 = 560.33$, $\text{df} = 6$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$), and in Nemenyi comparisons pooled over both spillover regimes, Incidence-Guided Saturation ranked significantly better than every other design and than SRS. This pooled ranking rests on its advantage under control-only spillover. Under both-arms spillover its MSE was 8\% above that of SRS (next section). Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons} gives the pairwise results.

## Design Performance by Spillover Regime

Of the factors varied, only the spillover regime changed the queen ranking at $\beta = 1$ (Table \ref{tab:grid-srs}, Figure \ref{fig:mse}). Under the both-arms regime, Balanced Quartiles had the lowest MSE (0.042), followed by Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.046), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.062), Checkerboard (0.062), Isolation Buffer (0.161), and High Incidence Focus (0.162). Under the control-only regime, the order was Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.135), Isolation Buffer (0.159), Balanced Quartiles (0.219), High Incidence Focus (0.329), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.576), and Checkerboard (2.111). At larger values of $\beta$, Isolation Buffer matched or passed Incidence-Guided Saturation under this regime (see @sec-tau).

For Isolation Buffer, no treated cluster has a treated neighbor, which means $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z} = 0$ at every treated cluster and $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z} \circ (\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z}$. Therefore, the two regimes in Equation \ref{eq:spillover} define the same outcome model and the same expected MSE. The observed values, 0.161 and 0.159, differ only by Monte Carlo error because the two regimes use separate draws. Every other design had a higher MSE under the control-only regime. The increase was largest for Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking, which went from close to the best designs under the both-arms regime to the two worst under the control-only regime.

Among the six detailed designs, Incidence-Guided Saturation was first or second under both regimes, at this and every other value of $\beta$. However, in the full benchmark that includes SRS (Table \ref{tab:grid-srs}), its both-arms MSE was 8\% above that of SRS, a small but statistically detectable difference (Figure \ref{fig:vs-srs}).

The increase under the control-only regime was variance, not bias. The oracle model includes the true regime-specific spillover covariate. Therefore, it has no omitted-variable bias. At $\beta = 1$, in every combination of design and regime under queen contiguity, the absolute bias was at most 0.048 and squared bias, averaged over scenarios, was at most 2.2\% of MSE. Checkerboard showed the mechanism most clearly: under the control-only regime its spillover covariate is a linear combination of the intercept and $\mathbf{Z}$ at every interior cluster, which means only the boundary clusters separate the spillover effect from the treatment effect (Appendix \ref{app:technical}). Checkerboard's MSE rose from 0.062 under the both-arms regime to 2.111 under the control-only regime, while its bias stayed near zero (0.004) and its coverage stayed at 0.951, because its intervals widened with its variance. Its pooled MSE of 1.087 was almost entirely variance, and squared bias, averaged over scenarios, was 0.004, less than 0.5\% of MSE. Figure \ref{fig:biasvar} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures} shows the decomposition for the Poisson configuration with $\rho_X = 0.20$. $2\times2$ Blocking showed the same pattern on a smaller scale, with MSE rising from 0.062 to 0.576 and a bias of 0.016 under the control-only regime.

## Sampling Designs Compared to Simple Random Sampling {#sec-vs-srs}

At $\beta=1$ under queen contiguity, pooled over the five incidence configurations and all spatial and spillover settings, Incidence-Guided Saturation had mean MSE 0.091 against 0.128 for SRS, and Saturation Quadrants had 0.090. Table \ref{tab:grid-srs} separates the regimes for all eight designs and SRS. Figure \ref{fig:grid-srs} shows the six detailed designs and SRS with the five incidence configurations kept separate. Within each regime the configurations lie close together for every design, but the regime changes how each design compares with SRS. Incidence-Guided Saturation's MSE was 0.631 times that of SRS under control-only spillover and 1.083 times under both arms. SRS, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves had similar both-arms accuracy, although small differences in means do not establish equivalence. The design guidance differs between the regimes, and pooling over them would obscure that difference.

Figure \ref{fig:vs-srs} tests each design against SRS within each regime, over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. Under control-only spillover, Incidence-Guided Saturation had 36.9\% lower MSE than SRS (95\% interval 34.5\% to 39.2\% lower), Saturation Quadrants 36.7\% lower and Isolation Buffer 25.7\% lower, each in all 50 units (Holm-adjusted $p = 6.2\times10^{-9}$). Under both-arms spillover, Incidence-Guided Saturation had 8.3\% higher MSE than SRS (5.6\% to 11.0\% higher, $p = 6.1\times10^{-6}$) and Saturation Quadrants 4.3\% higher ($p = 0.017$). Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves did not differ significantly from SRS under either regime. Isolation Buffer, High Incidence Focus, $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard had significantly higher MSE than SRS under both-arms spillover. High Incidence Focus, $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard also had significantly higher MSE under control-only spillover.

Under rook contiguity the saturation designs had 23\% to 24\% lower control-only MSE than SRS and 3\% to 5\% higher both-arms MSE, significant for Incidence-Guided Saturation ($p = 0.0075$) but not for Saturation Quadrants ($p = 0.15$). Isolation Buffer's control-only MSE under rook contiguity was 5.8\% higher than that of SRS.

## Robustness to Incidence Pattern, Spatial Dependence and Spillover Magnitude {#sec-config}

Table \ref{tab:by-config} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables} gives each design's MSE within each of the five incidence configurations. Under queen contiguity, the mean-MSE order within every configuration was the same as the pooled order: Incidence-Guided Saturation, Balanced Quartiles, Isolation Buffer, High Incidence Focus, $2\times2$ Blocking, and Checkerboard. The configuration changed each design's MSE only slightly. In this order, each design's highest MSE across the five configurations was lower than the next design's lowest. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest MSE in 18 to 21 of the 32 blocks in each configuration. Coverage did not depend on the configuration either: within each configuration, every design's coverage, averaged over its 32 scenarios, was between 0.941 and 0.952. High Incidence Focus, the design that uses the incidence ranks most directly, did not have higher MSE under the two Poisson configurations than under the iid and spatial configurations.

Under queen contiguity, neither the strength of spatial dependence in the outcome nor the spillover magnitude changed the ranking. Across $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$, no design's MSE changed by more than 0.020. Across $\psi \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, the MSE of every design except Checkerboard also varied by less than 0.020, and Checkerboard's varied between 1.052 and 1.108 with no trend in $\psi$ (Table \ref{tab:psi} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables}). Under rook contiguity, $\psi$ mattered for Checkerboard alone, for the reason given in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}.

Table \ref{tab:robustness} gives the distribution of MSE across the 160 queen blocks at $\beta = 1$. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest median (0.080) and the lowest worst-case MSE of any design (0.169). Isolation Buffer had the narrowest range (0.128 to 0.206), because its MSE does not depend on the spillover regime, but at a higher median than the two leading designs. Balanced Quartiles had a low median (0.115) and a worst case of 0.290. The distributions of $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard reflected their dependence on the spillover regime: both had low first quartiles (0.062 and 0.063) and high upper quartiles (0.580 and 2.093). Checkerboard had the highest MSE in all 80 control-only blocks. In the 80 both-arms blocks, the highest MSE belonged to High Incidence Focus in 42 and to Isolation Buffer in 38. Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation also had the lowest worst-case MSE (0.138). These worst cases summarize variation across parameter settings, not the conditional risk across assignments within one setting.

## Stability Across Treatment Effect Sizes {#sec-tau}

Under queen contiguity, the order of the designs by mean MSE and the order by average within-block rank were each the same at every $\beta \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$ (Figure \ref{fig:tau-mse}a), and with SRS included, average rank placed SRS second at every value of $\beta$. Under rook contiguity the order was also stable (Figure \ref{fig:tau-mse}b), except that the close pair of $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer swapped order at $\beta = 3$. The five values of $\beta$ share their assignments and noise. Therefore, these comparisons are not independent confirmations of one another.

\centering

Each point averages the 160 scenarios of one design at one value of $\beta$, pooled over the five incidence configurations. Shaded bands show $\pm 1$ times the average of the scenario-level Monte Carlo standard errors of MSE. They describe the precision of a single scenario's MSE, not of the plotted average, whose standard error is smaller (Table \ref{tab:performance}). The shared legend lists the designs in order of pooled mean MSE under queen contiguity at $\beta = 1$. The vertical scales of the two panels differ. The gray dashed line marks simple random sampling (SRS). Checkerboard under rook contiguity is flagged because $\beta$ is not identifiable (Section~\ref{sec-estimation}). \label{fig:tau-mse}

Within that order, Isolation Buffer closed the gap on Incidence-Guided Saturation under control-only spillover. There, the MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.131 at $\beta = 0.8$ to 0.182 at $\beta = 3$, while that of Isolation Buffer stayed between 0.159 and 0.160. The two were level at $\beta = 2$ (0.160 each), and at $\beta = 3$ Isolation Buffer had the lower control-only MSE. Incidence-Guided Saturation remained lowest in pooled MSE at every value of $\beta$, and the rise in its MSE was mostly variance: squared bias stayed at or below 3.0\% of its MSE. Appendix \ref{app:technical-notes} traces the rise to a term of the estimation error that grows with $\beta$ when treated clusters have treated neighbors. Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation kept the lowest control-only MSE at every value of $\beta$, although its margin over Isolation Buffer narrowed from 0.095 against 0.134 at $\beta = 0.8$ to 0.131 against 0.136 at $\beta = 3$.

Coverage stayed between 0.946 and 0.952 at every value of $\beta$ for every design except Checkerboard under rook contiguity. Its coverage rose from 0.150 at $\beta = 0.8$ to 0.464 at $\beta = 3$ because its intervals widened around an estimate of $\beta - \psi$ rather than $\beta$ (Appendix \ref{app:technical-notes}).

## Allocation-Specific Risk on the Grid

Under control-only spillover, the worst 10\% of SRS allocations on the grid had mean conditional MSE 60\% above that of the average SRS allocation (0.346 against 0.217). For the two saturation designs, the worst-decile MSE under control-only spillover was 0.54 to 0.55 times SRS's on the grid. Under both-arms spillover, it was 1.06 to 1.07 times SRS's on the grid.

Averaged over the 200 units per regime (fixed surfaces crossed with the extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\psi$), Incidence-Guided Saturation's control-only mean MSE was 0.140 against 0.217 for SRS. Its estimated 90th percentile of allocation-specific MSE was 0.173 against 0.296, and its estimated worst-decile mean was 0.191 against 0.346, lower than SRS in all 200 units on both measures. Under both arms, the corresponding mean MSE was 0.046 against 0.043 and the worst-decile mean 0.058 against 0.054. Saturation Quadrants showed a similar reduction under control-only spillover. Table \ref{tab:downside} in @sec-application compares every design with SRS on both criteria. These results come from the extreme parameter settings only and give qualified support to saturation on downside risk. The precision check preserved the control-only direction, but outcome noise contributed substantially to the estimated variation across allocations, especially under both arms: it accounted for a median 63\% of the variance of Incidence-Guided Saturation's estimated risk under control-only spillover and 92\% under both arms. Quantiles and worst-decile membership estimated from a finite number of outcomes remain uncertain. The grid study did not use split-half selection. Therefore, its worst-decile means are biased upward for every design, most for designs whose estimated risk is mostly outcome noise. Instead of extrapolating the size of the tail protection from these settings, we use the NC case study in @sec-application as a setting-specific assessment.

# Case Study: Simulation Based on Sudden Unexpected Death in North Carolina {#sec-application}

This section evaluates the designs in a case study that uses simulation with observed North Carolina incidence to recommend a design for the statewide extension of the SUD-prevention education pilot trial. It uses the outcome model, designs, estimator and performance criteria of @sec-methods. The first four subsections describe the observed inputs and the changes this setting requires, and the last three report the results.

## Purpose, Observed Inputs and Simulated Outcomes

The case study asks which allocation designs estimate a known education-intervention effect accurately on this geography, when some designs use historical SUD incidence to direct treatment. It informs the choice of design for a statewide extension of a pilot trial of education for healthcare professionals involved in SUD prevention. Observed incidence and geography are fixed inputs, and the outcomes are simulated. The case study uses no observed intervention outcomes and no estimated relationship between local SUD incidence and education performance. Any eventual effect on SUD incidence requires a separate clinical evaluation. A real trial realizes only one allocation per planning year. Therefore, both average estimation error and the risk of a poor allocation matter.

The assignment units are 58 community college service-area clusters that partition North Carolina's 100 counties under the study mapping (Figure \ref{fig:service-areas}). The county-to-college assignments are analysis conventions, not exclusive service commitments (Appendix \ref{app:nc}). Observed county-year deaths at ages 18--64, and population estimates for the same ages from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results program [@seer_population_data], were aggregated to the same named clusters for each year, 2018--2021. SUD deaths were identified from death certificates with the case-adjudication algorithm of Gan and colleagues [@gan_factors_2019]. We used the corrected numerator supplied by Habib [@habib_temporal_2026], which includes heart-failure deaths formerly excluded as presumed non-sudden and totals 23,523 deaths over 25,594,321 person-years (Appendix \ref{app:nc}).

Annual incidence is $100,000D_{iy}/P_{iy}$, and pooled incidence is $100,000\sum_yD_{iy}/\sum_yP_{iy}$, with the latter population sum interpreted as person-years. All 58 clusters are present in each year, and counts and populations sum back to statewide totals. We held these observed annual surfaces fixed, generated no synthetic incidence surface and report years separately (Figure \ref{fig:nc-observed}). The county death-certificate source data are restricted and not publicly available. We report only 58-cluster summaries. The data were obtained under University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Institutional Review Board protocol 14-2036, "Sudden Unexpected Death in North Carolina" (principal investigator Ross J. Simpson, Jr., Department of Medicine).

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]

\centering

## Design Adaptations to the North Carolina Map

Queen contiguity between service areas, computed from legal county boundaries, defines primary adjacency, and rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis. Shared legal boundaries across water can create adjacency. Adjacency here is a prespecified geographic proxy for exposure, not a measured network of professional communication.

All eight designs and SRS are evaluated under the names used on the grid, adapted to the irregular map. Appendix \ref{app:nc} gives the rules in full and maps the fixed regions and example assignments. Checkerboard becomes a deterministic rule that visits clusters from most to fewest neighbors and gives each cluster the arm held by fewer of its already-assigned neighbors, an approximation of strict interspersion rather than an exact checkerboard. High Incidence Focus treats the 29 highest annual-rate clusters, and Isolation Buffer draws a greedy random maximal independent set on the NC adjacency graph. SRS treats a random 29 of 58 clusters, and Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves stratify annual rate ranks and treat 29 overall.

The two saturation designs use one fixed four-region partition for all years. We ran $k$-means clustering [@hartigan_algorithm_1979] on the cluster coordinates 250 times and kept the partition that best balanced compactness, population, number of clusters and number of counties, without consulting outcomes. Saturation Quadrants randomly assigns 20/40/60/80\% to these regions in each draw. Incidence-Guided Saturation ranks the regions by the mean rank of their clusters' annual per-capita rates and assigns 80/60/40/20\% from highest to lowest. Mean raw rates and pooled regional rates serve as prespecified alternative regional summaries.

On the NC map, $2\times2$ Blocking becomes spatial blocking. Each year, we form 14 groups of similar nearby clusters by $k$-means clustering (25 starts) on four standardized variables: the cluster coordinates, that year's incidence rank and log population. Half of each group, rounded to the nearest even whole number (1.5 to 2, 0.5 to 0), is treated at random. Therefore, treatment budgets, the numbers of treated clusters, differ across designs. We report them (Table \ref{tab:nc-budgets}) rather than modify the designs to force equal budgets.

## Outcome Model and Evaluation {#sec-nc-outcome}

For the primary education outcome, we set $\tau=0$ in Equation \ref{eq:outcome}, use the 58-cluster $\mathbf{W}$, and fix $\beta=1$, $\sigma=1$:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{I}-\rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}[\beta \mathbf{Z}+\psi\,\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z})+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}],\qquad \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).
\end{equation*}
Observed incidence affects assignments but does not shift the simulated education outcome or the constant intervention effect. We estimated $\beta$ with the same validated maximum likelihood implementation as in the grid study, with an intercept, $\mathbf{Z}$ and the true regime-specific $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z})$, without $\mathbf{X}$. As in the grid model, $\beta$ is the coefficient before spatial propagation, not an average total effect after applying $(\mathbf{I}-\rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}$. For the main case study and for the analyses of partial participation and sample size below, we report $\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975,\,N-p}\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\sqrt{N/(N-p)}$, where $N$ is the number of participating colleges ($N = 58$ in the main case study) and $p$ the number of fitted coefficients plus $\rho$. We tested $\beta = 0$ two-sided at level 0.05, rejecting when the 95\% interval excluded zero. Grid power (@sec-simulation) is one-sided at level 0.025. The maximum likelihood variance divides by $N$, and the normal reference distribution ignores the estimated parameters. With 58 or fewer clusters, both make the Wald interval too narrow.

Primary queen settings cross $\rho=0,0.2,0.5$, $\psi=0.5,0.8$, both regimes, four years and nine designs (432 reported settings). A matched hypothetical sensitivity analysis lets incidence shift the simulated outcome and adds incidence to the fitted model. It adds $\mathbf{X}=(\operatorname{rank}_{\rm average}(\text{rate})-0.5)/58$ with $\tau=1$ to both the simulated outcome and the fitted covariates (432 settings). It changes the outcome and the adjustment together and is not an empirical association between incidence and education. A rook-contiguity sensitivity analysis of the primary model uses the extreme values $\rho=0,0.5$ (288 settings), and the two alternative regional summaries add 96 Incidence-Guided Saturation settings. The full case study reports 1,248 settings, computed from 936 distinct simulation settings, because reported settings with the same allocations and outcome model share one simulation.

We sampled $J=100$ assignments and simulated $R=100$ independent outcomes per distinct assignment. A design with only one possible assignment instead received $R=1,000$ outcomes for that assignment, rather than 100 repeated copies of it counted as separate allocations. A prespecified adaptive schedule extended allocations or outcomes where needed until the Monte Carlo standard error of mean MSE was at most 5\% of mean MSE and that of coverage at most 0.01. Two single-assignment settings in the matched sensitivity analysis required $R=2,000$, and all randomized designs met these targets at $J=100$ and $R=100$ (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}). In the primary model, Checkerboard, Saturation Quadrants, Isolation Buffer and SRS reuse the same simulations across years because annual incidence enters neither their allocation nor the outcome model. As a result, their repeated values are not independent annual confirmations.

For each allocation $a$, the repeated outcomes estimate the conditional MSE $m(a)=E_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}[(\hat\beta-\beta)^2\mid a,\text{observed inputs}]$, the expected squared error of the estimate if $a$ were the allocation realized. We report its distribution across sampled allocations, its estimated 90th percentile and the estimated mean among the worst 10\% of sampled allocations, alongside unconditional mean MSE, bias and coverage. A separate refinement of the tail estimates at queen $\rho=0,0.5$, $\psi=0.8$, both regimes and all years and designs kept the same allocations and extended the randomized designs to $R=400$ outcomes per allocation, keeping $R=1,000$ for single-assignment designs. The reported worst-decile means use all simulated outcomes for each assignment, which can overstate them by selecting on outcome noise. As a check, we also identified the worst decile with one half of the outcomes and evaluated it with the other half. We recorded design-matrix rank, residual treatment information, aliased columns, warnings, invalid estimates or intervals, and boundary estimates of $\rho$.

We compared the nine designs with the Friedman, Nemenyi and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests used on the grid, treating the 24 combinations of year, $\rho$ and $\psi$ as blocks, separately for each spillover regime and each value of $\tau$. The four years share one map and the designs whose allocations ignore annual incidence share their simulations across years, which means these $p$-values summarize consistency rather than independent evidence.

In further sensitivity analyses, we fit conditional autoregressive (CAR) and Bayesian models and replaced the proportional spillover exposure by binary and count forms (Appendices \ref{app:nc-ext} and \ref{app:nc-ext-results}).

## Partial Participation and Sample Size

We assume that all 58 colleges would be invited to take part after the pilot and that not every college would join. Therefore, we repeated the case study for subsets of $N$ participating colleges, $N \in \{15, 20, 25, 29, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 58\}$, under the education outcome model with $\tau = 0$. Under random volunteering, 50 subsets were drawn for each $N$ and shared by every design and year, giving a comparison of the designs on the same participants. In a sensitivity analysis at $N = 20$ and $N = 29$, a college's chance of joining rose linearly with its incidence rank, and the highest-incidence college was three times as likely to join as the lowest. Each design was rebuilt on the participants with its own rule, and the four saturation regions were required to contain at least two colleges each.

Spatial dependence links participating colleges only, which means a participant with no participating neighbor has a zero row in the participants' weights matrix $\mathbf{W}_P$. Spillover exposure counts treated participating neighbors over all geographic neighbors, $e_j(\mathbf{Z}) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(j)} Z_k / |\mathcal{N}(j)|$, and a non-participating neighbor counts as untreated.

Spillover scales with the effect, $\psi = \kappa\beta$ with $\kappa \in \{0.5, 0.8\}$, and the effect $\beta$ took nine values from 0 to 2 in units of the college-level outcome standard deviation. Tying $\psi$ to $\beta$ means that an intervention with no effect also has no spillover, which the size calculation at $\beta = 0$ requires, and keeps the ratio of spillover to direct effect the same along each power curve. Settings crossed these with $\rho \in \{0, 0.5\}$, both spillover regimes, the nine designs and the four planning years.

With fewer than 58 participants, each setting used 20 allocations and 10 outcomes on each of the 50 subsets (10,000 fits), and a design with a single possible allocation on a subset used 200 outcomes instead. With all 58 colleges, each setting used 100 allocations and 100 outcomes, as in the main case study, and reproduced that case study's MSE and coverage within Monte Carlo error. All effect sizes share the same subsets, allocations and noise, which makes power curves smooth in $\beta$. For each setting we estimated three quantities with the corrected $t$ test above: power, the number of colleges needed for 80\% power, and the smallest effect detectable with 80\% power at each $N$.

Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext} translates college-level effects into individual-level standardized effects through the intracluster correlation and the number of trained professionals per college, $n_c$.

## Accuracy, Coverage and Share of Population Treated

Every setting met its prespecified precision targets for mean MSE and coverage, with no warnings, aliased columns, boundary estimates of $\rho$ or estimation failures (run sizes in Appendix \ref{app:nc-results}).

Figure \ref{fig:nc-mse} compares the eight designs with SRS by year and regime. Under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants had mean MSE 0.223 against 0.308 for SRS, a 27.4\% reduction. Incidence-Guided Saturation reduced mean MSE by 21.1--29.9\% across the four observed years (Table \ref{tab:nc-year} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-results}). Under control-only spillover, both saturation designs had lower mean MSE than SRS in every primary parameter setting, and approximate Monte Carlo intervals for each setting-specific difference excluded zero. Neither design was uniquely best, and as on the grid the two performed similarly. The performance of High Incidence Focus under control-only spillover depended on the year. As a result, we cannot recommend it for every year.

Under both-arms spillover, SRS mean MSE was 0.076, Saturation Quadrants 0.075, and Incidence-Guided Saturation 0.074 to 0.077 across years. SRS remained competitive with balancing, blocking and saturation. High Incidence Focus had low both-arms MSE in the primary model, but its allocation is deterministic for these fixed rates. Its low MSE reflects model-based accuracy conditional on that allocation and does not show that the design has the protection that randomization provides.

Mean coverage of the 95\% $t$-based intervals across the four years was between 0.941 and 0.949 for all nine designs and both regimes, and between 0.941 and 0.951 in single years. The Wald interval covered only 0.926 to 0.936 for the same nine designs. Table \ref{tab:interval-comparison} compares the two intervals for the six designs and SRS. Meeting the Monte Carlo precision targets did not repair that finite-sample undercoverage, but the corrected $t$ interval described in @sec-nc-outcome did (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}). Appendix \ref{app:nc-results} gives bias and coverage for every year, design and regime. Checkerboard's treatment effect is identifiable on this irregular graph, but weak separation of the treatment and spillover effects makes its estimates imprecise. On the rectangular grid under rook contiguity, by contrast, $\beta$ is not identifiable for Checkerboard.

Table \ref{tab:nc-budgets} also gives the share of the population that each design reaches. High Incidence Focus treats 29 clusters but only about 22--24\% of the working-age population, while Isolation Buffer treats a mean of 15.89 clusters and about 27\%. These population denominators measure geographic reach, not the number of healthcare professionals educated, intervention cost or participant-level precision.

Incidence-Guided Saturation assigns more treatment to high-incidence regions when incidence differs between regions. On the NC map incidence differs little between regions, because the four regions' mean incidence ranks lie between 24 and 34 of 58 in every year. On average, Incidence-Guided Saturation treated colleges holding 51.1\% of the summed college incidence rates, against 50.4\% for Saturation Quadrants and 62.2\% for High Incidence Focus. The shares of deaths showed the opposite pattern (49.2\%, 49.6\% and 35.4\%) because the highest-rate colleges serve small populations. On the simulation grid, where regional incidence differed more, incidence guidance raised the treated share of incidence by 2.1 to 3.1 percentage points over Saturation Quadrants. Across surfaces, the gain rose with the spread of the regions' mean incidence ranks (correlation 0.84 to 0.99).

## Allocation-Specific Risk in North Carolina

At the two refined queen settings, $\rho=0$ and $\rho=0.5$ with $\psi=0.8$, under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants' estimated 90th percentile of allocation-specific MSE was 31.8--32.9\% below SRS and its estimated worst-decile mean 34.6--37.8\% below. Incidence-Guided Saturation's corresponding reductions were 20.8--38.6\% and 20.7--43.4\%. The pattern persisted under the split-half evaluation described above. Figure \ref{fig:nc-risk} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-results} shows the $\rho=0.5$ setting. These reductions suggest a benefit for downside risk as well as for average error, under the studied model and sampled assignments.

Table \ref{tab:downside} compares every design with SRS on both criteria, mean conditional MSE and the mean of the worst 10\% of sampled allocations, on the grid and at the refined NC settings. Under control-only spillover, both saturation designs had lower mean and worst-decile MSE than SRS in both settings. Isolation Buffer also had a lower worst decile than SRS under control-only spillover (0.62 of SRS on the grid and 0.91 in NC). Under both-arms spillover, its mean was 3.80 and 3.69 times that of SRS, and it treated fewer clusters. High Incidence Focus has a single allocation in NC. That allocation's MSE was below the SRS worst-decile mean under both regimes (0.76 under both arms and 0.64 under control-only spillover), with mean MSE close to SRS (0.93 and 1.03). However, on the grid its both-arms mean was 3.81 times that of SRS, and its NC result depends on the incidence model, as the matched sensitivity analysis below shows. Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves matched SRS on both criteria. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking did not improve on SRS on either criterion in any setting.
