The tail estimates remain uncertain. With $J=100$ the worst decile contains only ten sampled draws, and every reported setting in the tail refinement for designs with more than one possible assignment flags uncertain worst-decile membership. Under both arms, the two outcome halves selected largely different worst deciles (a Jaccard index, the number of sampled assignments in both worst deciles divided by the number in either, of 0 to 0.25 for Incidence-Guided Saturation), and about 61--86\% of the variance of estimated risk across allocations came from outcome Monte Carlo noise, which means small both-arms tail differences do not establish better downside protection. Checkerboard and High Incidence Focus each have only one possible assignment in this setting. They show no spread across assignments, but that does not mean their error is low.

In the matched hypothetical sensitivity analysis, which lets incidence shift the simulated outcome and adjusts for it, High Incidence Focus MSE rose to roughly 3.68--4.44 times its primary value under both arms and 1.42--2.52 times under control-only spillover. This design treats the highest-incidence clusters. Therefore, adjusting for incidence leaves less variation in treatment that is independent of incidence. Comparing rook and queen contiguity at the same extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\psi$ leaves the regime-specific conclusions broadly unchanged. For Incidence-Guided Saturation, the matched ratios of sensitivity MSE to primary MSE ranged from 0.907 to 1.133 across the four planning years, both regimes, and the incidence-shift, rook and two alternative regional-summary analyses. Alternative regional summaries change the regional ordering in some years. Where an alternative summary gives the same ordering and ties, it gives the same set of possible assignments and the same results. We retain the prespecified mean-rank rule rather than select a summary retrospectively. Appendix \ref{app:nc} reports the regional ordering.

The design comparison did not depend on the spatial model used to generate or fit the data, with one exception (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}). Fitting a CAR model, generating the data from a CAR model, or both, left the saturation designs with 0.76 to 0.82 times SRS's MSE under control-only spillover. Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer were still the worst designs under both-arms spillover.

A Bayesian spatial lag model reproduced the maximum likelihood results, with posterior means correlated 0.999 with the maximum likelihood estimates, credible-interval coverage of 0.946 to 0.953 and the same design ordering.

The exception is a CAR model fit to data from the spatial lag model with strong spatial dependence ($\rho = 0.5$). Under the spatial lag model the outcome mean includes the spatial multiplier. Therefore, the CAR coefficient on treatment estimates a different quantity from $\beta$ [@wall_close_2004]. The maximum likelihood CAR estimates were biased by 0.110 under both-arms spillover and 0.205 under control-only spillover. The Bayesian CAR estimates were biased by 0.138 to 0.219 even when the chains converged, with coverage of 0.88 to 0.90, and they did not reproduce the saturation designs' control-only advantage. The correctly specified Bayesian spatial lag model does not share the problem.

Under a binary spillover exposure Isolation Buffer was never identifiable, and under a count exposure the saturation designs still had the lowest MSE under control-only spillover. Formal tests over the 24 combinations of year, $\rho$ and $\psi$ rejected equal ranks for every regime and value of $\tau$ (Friedman $\chi^2$ from 135 to 180 on 8 degrees of freedom). Under control-only spillover, the two saturation designs had the two best average ranks.

## Power Analysis for Partial Participation {#sec-nc-colleges}

Under both-arms spillover, the design affected the number of colleges a trial needs only for Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer. Every other design needed 35 to 37 colleges for 80\% power to detect a college-level effect of one standard deviation, and about 19 colleges for 1.5 standard deviations (Figure \ref{fig:colleges-needed}, Table \ref{tab:nc-power}). Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer did not reach 80\% power at $\beta = 1$ even with all 58 colleges.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_colleges_needed.pdf}
\caption[Number of participating colleges needed for 80\% power with the corrected $t$ test]{Number of participating colleges needed for 80\% power with the corrected $t$ test, by design, for a college-level effect of $\beta = 1$ standard deviation under both-arms spillover and $\beta = 1.5$ under control-only spillover, with random volunteering, $\rho = 0.5$ and $\psi = 0.8\beta$. Dark bars show the mean over the 2018--2021 planning years and whiskers the range. Light bars, drawn at 58, mark designs that did not reach 80\% power with all 58 colleges in at least one planning year. Their labels give the number of years, out of four, in which 58 colleges were not enough and, where 80\% power was reached in other years, the fewest colleges needed in those years.}
\label{fig:colleges-needed}
\end{figure}
```

Under control-only spillover, no design reached 80\% power at $\beta = 1$ with all 58 colleges. At $\beta = 1.5$ the two saturation designs needed 28 colleges, against 29 to 32 for SRS and the rank-based designs (High Incidence Focus, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves). At that effect, $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer failed to reach 80\% power with 58 colleges in one of the four planning years. Power under control-only spillover rose slowly beyond about 40 colleges (Figure \ref{fig:power-n} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-results}). When nearly every college participates, nearly every control has a treated neighbor, which means spillover exposure varies little and is hard to separate from treatment. Non-participating neighbors restore some of that variation, as do the saturation designs. With all 58 colleges, the smallest effect detectable with 80\% power under both-arms spillover was 0.76 to 0.78 college-level standard deviations for every design except Checkerboard (1.32) and Isolation Buffer (1.50). Under control-only spillover it was 1.24 to 1.25 for the two saturation designs, against 1.45 to 1.57 for SRS and the rank-based designs.

A college-level effect of $\beta$ standard deviations corresponds to an individual-level standardized effect $d = \beta\sigma_c$, where $\sigma_c = \sqrt{\text{ICC} + (1 - \text{ICC})/n_c}$ is the standard deviation of a college mean of $n_c$ professionals' scores and ICC is the intracluster correlation coefficient. Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results} gives example powers for individual-level effects (Table \ref{tab:nc-translation}). Letting the number of professionals grow with college population, at the same average of 25 used there, reduced power by 0.097 on average across designs, settings and effect sizes and changed no design's relative standing.

The Wald test rejected a true null hypothesis in 11\% to 13\% of simulated trials with 15 colleges and in 6\% to 7\% with 58. With the corrected $t$ test the rejection rate was 4.4\% to 5.6\%. The coverage of the corrected interval at $\beta = 1$ was between 0.940 and 0.956 for every design and regime at every number of colleges (Table \ref{tab:nc-calibration} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}). Therefore, the colleges-needed numbers above come from a test with the nominal size.

The regime-specific guidance held with fewer participants, but the size of the saturation advantage depended on participation (Table \ref{tab:nc-guidance} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}). Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer remained worse than SRS under both-arms spillover at every number of colleges, and the rank-based designs' mean MSE was within 2\% of that of SRS, except High Incidence Focus with 40 and 58 colleges (4\% and 8\% below). Under control-only spillover, the saturation designs' mean MSE was 22\% below that of SRS with 58 colleges, 9\% to 10\% below with 40, 4\% to 5\% below with 29 and about 1\% below with 20. With few participants, non-participating neighbors already create the exposure variation that saturation otherwise supplies. When the colleges with higher incidence were more likely to volunteer, the saturation designs' advantage over SRS was 2\% or less at 20 and 29 colleges. Isolation Buffer went from matching SRS under control-only spillover with 58 colleges to 2.3 times SRS's MSE with 29 colleges and 6.2 times with 15.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Interpretation of the Results

### Summary of Findings

We compared six treatment assignment designs, two related variants and SRS for a spatial cluster randomized trial on a 100-cluster grid, across three mechanisms of heterogeneous incidence, two spillover regimes and a range of values for spatial dependence, spillover magnitude and the treatment effect, and then in a case study on the North Carolina map. Each design was judged on its average MSE and on the spread of MSE across the allocations it can produce, the two criteria Chapter 2 used for SRS and Checkerboard on small grids, applied here to more designs, a larger grid, heterogeneous incidence and an irregular map. A trial realizes one allocation, and a design with a low average MSE can still give a poor estimate if some of its allocations perform badly.

Several findings held across the incidence configurations and the values of $\rho$, $\psi$ and $\beta$ under queen contiguity. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest pooled MSE and Balanced Quartiles the second lowest under both neighbor types, and the mechanism that generated incidence did not change the order. Coverage of the $t$-based intervals was close to 0.95 for every design whose $\beta$ was identifiable. Therefore, the designs differed in precision rather than in coverage.

At $\beta = 1$, the spillover regime was the one factor that changed the ranking. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking were among the best designs when spillover reached both arms and the two worst when it reached only control clusters, and Balanced Quartiles also ranked lower under control-only spillover. Incidence-Guided Saturation was first or second among the six designs under both regimes, although its both-arms MSE was 8\% above that of SRS. A trial team may not know the regime in advance. For a design whose performance depends on the regime, average MSE across regimes understates the risk of choosing it.

### Design Guidance by Spillover Regime

When spillover is expected to reach mainly control clusters, Incidence-Guided Saturation and Saturation Quadrants had the lowest mean MSE and among the lowest worst-decile MSE (Table \ref{tab:downside}). Therefore, they are the designs to consider first in that setting. This guidance assumes that most colleges take part, as the main analysis does. With 30 or fewer participating colleges, their advantage was 5\% or less (@sec-nc-colleges). Isolation Buffer also limited downside in that regime, but it should be considered only when both-arms spillover is implausible and a smaller treated budget is acceptable. When spillover is expected to reach both arms, the spread of MSE across allocations was small for SRS and the balancing and saturation designs. SRS, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves performed about equally. The saturation designs had mean MSE 4\% to 8\% above SRS on the grid and within 3\% of it in NC, with worst-decile MSE within 7\% of SRS's in both. Therefore, SRS and the saturation designs are both reasonable choices.

Incidence-Guided Saturation was not best in every setting. Under both-arms spillover its grid MSE was 8\% above that of SRS. Under control-only spillover its advantage narrowed as $\beta$ grew, and at $\beta = 3$ Isolation Buffer had the lower MSE (@sec-tau). In the case study, its advantage over SRS fell from 22\% with 58 colleges to about 1\% with 20, and it was 2\% or less at 20 and 29 colleges when high-incidence colleges were more likely to volunteer (@sec-nc-colleges).

The number of colleges a trial needs depends far more on the spillover regime than on the design. Under both-arms spillover, 35 to 37 colleges detect a one-standard-deviation college-level effect with any design except Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer. Under control-only spillover, even all 58 colleges do not reach 80\% power for a one-standard-deviation effect. The saturation designs' advantage over SRS also shrinks as fewer colleges join.

High Incidence Focus gave one fixed allocation whose MSE in NC was below the SRS worst-decile mean under both regimes. However, its accuracy is model-based rather than randomization-based. On the grid, its both-arms MSE was about four times that of SRS. There the fitted model adjusts for incidence, and a design that treats the highest-incidence half leaves little variation in treatment after that adjustment. The same happened in North Carolina when incidence shifted the outcome and entered the fitted model, where its MSE rose 1.4--4.4-fold. It is a candidate only when historical incidence can be assumed unrelated to the outcome. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking did not improve on SRS on either criterion.

Saturation Quadrants, which assigns the same saturations without reference to incidence, performed similarly to Incidence-Guided Saturation (@sec-vs-srs and Appendix \ref{app:eight-design}). Therefore, their accuracy advantage over SRS under control-only spillover appears to come from the shared saturation structure, and incidence guidance lets a trial direct its highest treatment saturations to the highest-incidence regions with little or no loss of estimation accuracy. How much treatment incidence guidance redirects depends on how much incidence differs between regions, a few percentage points of incidence share on the grid and less than one on the NC map, whose regions have similar incidence.

Before selecting one allocation, a trial team should weigh likely spillover, recruitment, cluster and participant budgets, achievable measurement precision and interval calibration.

## Limitations

The primary estimator is an oracle. It includes the exact spillover exposure term. Therefore, its results are a best case for each design. We fit a non-oracle model that omits the spillover term as a sensitivity analysis. It was biased for every design and its intervals under-covered, but Incidence-Guided Saturation still had the lowest MSE under both neighbor types. The non-oracle model is only one departure from the oracle. We did not study an analyst who includes a spillover term of the wrong form, such as one built on the wrong neighbor definition or a distance decay.

In the synthetic grid study, the designs and the fitted model used the incidence surface that generated the outcome (the matched-surface assumption in @sec-incidence). In practice, planning incidence is estimated from an earlier period and measured with error. The designs that assign treatment by incidence rank, and the covariate adjustment, would then use a noisy surface, and we did not study how that changes the comparison.

In the Poisson mechanism every cluster had the same population of 100,000. Real clusters, including the community college service areas in @sec-application, differ in population. Therefore, their observed rates differ in precision, and unequal populations may change how the designs that use incidence perform. In the case study, letting the number of trained professionals grow with college population reduced power by about 0.1 for every design and changed no design's relative standing.

The full synthetic comparison used one regular $10\times10$ grid, with $\tau$ and $\sigma$ fixed at 1. The case study added one irregular 58-cluster geography and unequal observed populations, but was not a systematic sweep over graph sizes, structures or participant budgets. Some grid results depend on its boundary geometry, and the design adaptations in the case study also change which assignments are possible. The designs compared came from design ideas developed for this trial and were not an exhaustive search of possible designs. The saturation designs used one set of saturations, 80\%, 60\%, 40\% and 20\%, and four regions. Other saturation sets and numbers of regions [@baird_optimal_2018] were not studied, and the saturation advantage under control-only spillover may depend on them.

The simulation shared random draws by design. Blocks within an incidence configuration share their surfaces, and the five values of $\beta$ and the case-study years share draws, which means these comparisons are not independent confirmations. The tests over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units address the shared surfaces within a configuration.

The simulation's base rate of 35 per 100,000 is not the rate of the county data (@sec-incidence). It is a general design study rather than a calibration, and in the Poisson mechanism the base rate matters only through the spatial pattern of the rank-scaled rates and the number of ties.

Case-study results are conditional on a continuous education-outcome model with known spillover form and constant structural effect, not an observed education intervention or demonstrated reduction in SUD. Working-age population is a geographic denominator rather than a sample of healthcare professionals. Historical rates are held fixed. Therefore, uncertainty in their measurement and changes between planning and implementation are not propagated. The matched sensitivity analysis in which incidence shifts the outcome is hypothetical.

The 95\% Wald intervals under-covered in both studies, and the Wald test was anti-conservative with few colleges. The $t$-based interval with a degrees-of-freedom-corrected standard error restored coverage to between 0.94 and 0.96 in the case study at every number of participating colleges (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results}) and to between 0.946 and 0.952 for every identifiable design on the grid. The allocation-tail estimates from a finite number of outcomes do not establish population worst cases, and the designs' budgets differ, which means these are evaluations of the retained designs, not an equal-cost optimization.

The participation analysis assumes that colleges volunteer at random or with probability rising with incidence, and that non-participating colleges neither transmit nor receive spillover.

## Future Work

The next trial-design steps will be to specify the education endpoint, the eligible professionals, the implementation budget and a plausible spillover network, and then to check interval calibration for that protocol before randomization.

The incidence coefficient $\tau$ was set by assumption here, at 1 on the grid and 0 in the case study. After a trial, it can be estimated from the trial data by including incidence as a covariate in the fitted model, and earlier trials or observational data on the same outcome could inform its value at the design stage. The value of 1 used on the grid may also need adjusting for other outcomes, for which incidence may shift the outcome by more or less than one noise standard deviation across its range.

Several extensions of the simulation would test how well the guidance generalizes. Chapter 2 used a binary spillover indicator, and the case study compared binary, count and proportional forms. The grid study could make the same comparison. Planning incidence measured with error, effect heterogeneity, exposure networks beyond contiguity and a broader set of graph geometries remain to be studied. A larger allocation sample would make the downside estimates more precise if a final choice depended on them.

Incidence-Guided Saturation outperformed SRS under control-only spillover with one set of saturations and four regions. Future work will vary the saturations and the number of regions to find whether another configuration estimates the intervention effect more accurately.

The trial endpoint here is a measured education score, an intermediate outcome. Designing for a later reduction in SUD incidence would need a count outcome model.

### Random-Number Streams {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Every random draw in the simulation has its own seed, computed by hashing a key that names the draw. The key lists the draw's type (incidence surface, assignments, or noise) and the parameters that identify it, with numeric values written to a fixed number of decimal places so that equal values always give the same key. The random-number generator and its methods for normal and discrete draws are also fixed explicitly, which means the streams do not depend on software defaults. @sec-simulation describes the consequences of this scheme: independence from the order of execution, and common random numbers.

### Monte Carlo Structure and Checkpoints {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Within a scenario, fit $(k, j)$, with $k = 1, \dots, 10$ and $j = 1, \dots, 25$, uses surface $\mathbf{X}_k$, assignment $\mathbf{Z}_{kj}$, and noise vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{kj}$, the $(k, j)$ column of the block's $100 \times 250$ noise matrix (see @sec-simulation). The unit of computation is a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, and $\rho$: 40 units, each covering 4 values of $\psi$, 2 spillover regimes, 8 designs, 5 values of $\beta$, 250 fits, and 2 estimators. The units ran in parallel, and the run was set to stop if any unit failed. Each unit's results are saved together with a record of the parameter settings, the simulation code, and the software versions that produced them. Saved results are reused only if all of these match the current run. Therefore, results from different code or settings are never combined.

### Scenario Metrics {.unnumbered .unlisted}

For one scenario and estimator, let $f = 1, \dots, n$ index the valid fits, those with a finite estimate and standard error (here every fit was valid and $n = 250$). Let $L_f, U_f = \hat\beta_f \mp t_{0.975,\,N-p}\,\widehat{\text{SE}}_f\sqrt{N/(N-p)}$, with $N = 100$ clusters and $p$ as defined in @sec-estimation (the Wald limits replace the multiplier by $z_{0.975} = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) \approx 1.96$), and let $\bar{\hat\beta} = n^{-1}\sum_f \hat\beta_f$. Then
$$
\text{Bias} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}(\hat\beta_f - \beta), \qquad
\text{SD} = \left\{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\left(\hat\beta_f - \bar{\hat\beta}\right)^2\right\}^{1/2}, \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}(\hat\beta_f - \beta)^2,
$$
$$
\text{Coverage} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}\{L_f \le \beta \le U_f\}, \qquad
\text{Power} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}\{L_f > 0\},
$$
so that $\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + (n-1)\,\text{SD}^2/n$.

### Surface-Level Standard Errors {.unnumbered .unlisted}

For $u \in \{\text{Bias}, \text{MSE}, \text{Coverage}, \text{Power}\}$, let $u_k$ be the same formula applied to the valid fits from surface $k$ (here all 25). With $K = 10$ and $s(a_1, \dots, a_K) = \{(K-1)^{-1}\sum_k (a_k - \bar a)^2\}^{1/2}$ the sample standard deviation,
$$
\text{SE}(u) = \frac{s(u_1, \dots, u_K)}{\sqrt{K}}, \qquad u \pm t_{0.975,\,K-1}\,\text{SE}(u).
$$
With 25 fits from each surface, $u = K^{-1}\sum_k u_k$. For two designs $d$ and $d'$ in the same block at the same $\beta$, the difference is paired at the surface level: with $\Delta_k = u_{d,k} - u_{d',k}$,
$$
\text{SE}(u_d - u_{d'}) = \frac{s(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_K)}{\sqrt{K}},
$$
with the same $t_{0.975,\,K-1}$ interval.

### Standard Errors Pooled Over Configurations {.unnumbered .unlisted}

For one design, neighbor type, and value of $\beta$, let $\mathcal{B}_c$ be the 32 blocks of configuration $c$ and $u_{b,k}$ the surface-$k$ metric in block $b$. The configuration-by-surface means and the pooled metric are
$$
\bar u_{c,k} = \frac{1}{32}\sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}_c} u_{b,k}, \qquad
\bar u = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{c=1}^{5}\sum_{k=1}^{10}\bar u_{c,k},
$$
where $\bar u$ equals the mean of the metric over the 160 scenarios, and
$$
\text{SE}(\bar u) = \frac{s(\{\bar u_{c,k}\})}{\sqrt{50}},
$$
with $s$ taken over the 50 values $\bar u_{c,k}$. These are the standard errors in Table \ref{tab:performance}. For two designs $d$ and $d'$ adjacent in the mean-MSE order (@sec-queen), let $D_{c,k} = \bar u_{d,c,k} - \bar u_{d',c,k}$ for $u = \text{MSE}$. The interval for the mean difference is $\bar D \pm t_{0.975,\,49}\, s(\{D_{c,k}\})/\sqrt{50}$, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the normal approximation, is applied to the 50 values $D_{c,k}$.

## A2. Identification Under Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A2}{app:technical}Two combinations of design and neighbor type weaken or remove the information that separates $\beta$ from the spillover term. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard gives $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}$ exactly, because every neighbor of a treated cluster is a control and every neighbor of a control is treated. Both spillover covariates then equal $\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}$, a linear combination of the intercept and $\mathbf{Z}$, which means $\beta$ is not identifiable. The fitting routine drops the aliased spillover column, and because $\psi(\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}) = \psi\mathbf{1} - \psi\mathbf{Z}$, the coefficient on $\mathbf{Z}$ estimates $\beta - \psi$. Chapter 2 noted the same consequence of exact collinearity between treatment and spillover exposure. The non-oracle model has no spillover column to drop, but its Checkerboard estimates under rook contiguity have the same defect.

Under queen contiguity, each of the 64 interior clusters has four treated and four control neighbors, which gives $(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z})_i = 1/2$ at every interior cluster $i$. Under the control-only regime the spillover covariate then equals $(1/2)(\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z})$ at those clusters, a linear combination of the intercept and $\mathbf{Z}$, and only the 36 clusters on the grid boundary contain information that separates it from the intercept and $\mathbf{Z}$. As a result, $\beta$ is identifiable, but imprecisely. In the both-arms regime, the spillover covariate is the constant $1/2$ at interior clusters, confounded with the intercept but not with $\mathbf{Z}$.

Isolation Buffer under rook contiguity can also, rarely, draw exactly the checkerboard pattern, a maximal independent set that equals one color class of the grid. This happened in 4 of its 40,000 rook draws and affected one fit in each of 20 scenarios, 4 at each value of $\beta$. We flag every fit in which the fitting routine reports an aliased column and every scenario in which some draw has $\text{rank}([\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z}]) < 3$. Aliased estimates are kept in all summaries. In the exhibits, we flag Checkerboard under rook contiguity, where every fit is aliased. The Isolation Buffer scenarios, each with one aliased fit among its 250, are noted here and carry no flag in the exhibits.

## A3. Estimation Error Depends on the Treatment Effect {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A3}{app:technical-notes}This section explains why the control-only MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation rises with $\beta$ while that of Isolation Buffer does not (@sec-tau). The numbers that involve $\hat\rho$ come from a re-run of every block for the six designs, both neighbor types and all five values of $\beta$ (2.4 million fits of the oracle model), which reproduced the stored results in all 9,600 scenarios. For one fit, let $\mathbf{V} = [\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}), \mathbf{X}_k]$ be the covariate matrix of the oracle model, $\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{I} - \rho \mathbf{W})^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{V}^{+} = (\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}^\top$, and write $[\mathbf{V}^{+}\mathbf{v}]_Z$ for the coefficient on $\mathbf{Z}$ when a vector $\mathbf{v}$ is regressed on the columns of $\mathbf{V}$. Given $\hat\rho$, the estimated coefficients are $\mathbf{V}^{+}(\mathbf{I} - \hat\rho \mathbf{W})\mathbf{Y}$, and
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta - \beta = [\mathbf{V}^{+}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}]_Z + (\rho - \hat\rho)\,h + \beta(\rho - \hat\rho)\,g, \qquad g = [\mathbf{V}^{+}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}]_Z,
\label{eq:error-decomposition}
\end{equation}
where $h$ collects the remaining terms, none of which involves $\beta$. The first term has mean zero. The last term is the error in $\hat\rho$ multiplied by $\beta$ and by $g$, the coefficient on $\mathbf{Z}$ when the lagged treatment $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}$ is regressed on the model's own covariates. Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} held on every re-run fit to within $4.2\times10^{-13}$.

In these fits $\hat\rho$ was biased downward by about 0.06 on average. A finite-sample bias of this estimator in spatial autoregressive models is known [@bao_finite-sample_2013], and we did not derive its size for this design. With $\rho - \hat\rho$ positive on average, the last term adds a positive bias and extra variance that both grow with $\beta$ for any design with $g > 0$. Under control-only spillover at $\rho = 0$, $g$ is close to the average share of treated neighbors among treated clusters: 0.57 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, whose treated clusters are concentrated in the high-saturation quadrants, and exactly 0 for Isolation Buffer, whose treated clusters have no treated neighbors. Under queen contiguity and control-only spillover, the variance of the last term rose from 0.008 at $\beta = 0.8$ to 0.061 at $\beta = 3$ for Incidence-Guided Saturation and stayed below 0.0002 for Isolation Buffer, which is why Isolation Buffer had the lower MSE at $\beta = 3$. Under both-arms spillover at $\rho = 0$, the lagged treatment $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z}$ is the spillover covariate itself, and $g = 0$ for every design.

The same term explains why the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity rose with $\beta$. Its coefficient on $\mathbf{Z}$ estimates $\beta - \psi$, and the error in $\hat\rho$ is multiplied by $\beta - \psi$, which widens its intervals as $\beta$ grows. Its coverage rose from 0.150 at $\beta = 0.8$ to 0.464 at $\beta = 3$.

## A4. Design Rules and Regions on the North Carolina Map {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A4}{app:nc}The primary case-study numbers come from the aggregate performance and allocation-risk summaries of the main run and of the separate tail refinement. Annual tables average the six queen parameter pairs equally, without pooled Monte Carlo intervals. Each random draw used a fixed, reproducible seed. An independent check recomputed performance from the stored fits and verified the annual treatment budgets, the regional orderings, and the allocations and outcomes reused from the main run in the tail refinement.

### Data Conventions {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Northampton is assigned to Halifax Community College, Bertie to Martin Community College, and Hertford alone to Roanoke-Chowan Community College. These county-to-college assignments are analysis conventions, not exclusive service commitments. The earlier numerator, which excluded heart-failure deaths, reproduces the totals behind Habib's unpublished report [@habib_temporal_2026], and the case study uses the corrected numerator described in @sec-application. We do not infer undocumented upstream exclusion rules or zip-code allocation from the received county panel.


### Design Adaptations {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Before simulation, we checked the 58-cluster row-standardized contiguity matrix $\mathbf{W}$, its binary adjacency and its row order against the boundary geometry. On the NC map, Checkerboard visits clusters by decreasing degree, chooses the arm that conflicts least with assigned neighbors, breaks equal conflicts toward control, and complements the assignment if more than half are treated. In Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves, odd-size strata receive their necessary extra treatments at random. In Balanced Halves, one half receives 14 treatments and the other 15, with the extra-treatment half chosen randomly. The four-region partition used by both saturation designs was selected from 250 candidates generated by a geographic $k$-means procedure on standardized projected coordinates, by compactness and balance in reference population, cluster count and county count, without consulting outcomes. Reference population is pooled person-years divided by four.

Incidence-Guided Saturation first ranks clusters by annual per-capita rates, averages their ranks equally within each region, ranks those four means, and assigns 80/60/40/20\% from highest to lowest. Regional ties are broken randomly per allocation, and local treatment counts are rounded under the retained design rules. Per-capita cluster rates already account for population size. Regional mean ranks weight clusters equally. Pooled regional rates, which are deaths divided by population, weight larger clusters more heavily. Mean raw rates and pooled regional rates are evaluated as prespecified sensitivities rather than chosen by performance. The grid rule averages $\mathbf{X}$ directly. Mean ranks align with its rank-scaled Poisson cases but are a deliberate adaptation for the case study, not the exact rule used for continuous grid incidence.

The 14 groups used by $2\times2$ Blocking are formed once per year by $k$-means on standardized projected coordinates, incidence ranks and log(1+population), then held fixed, and contain one to eight clusters. Half of each group, rounded, is treated at random, and the single-cluster group of each year remains control because half of one cluster rounds to zero. As a result, the yearly numbers of treated clusters for $2\times2$ Blocking are 28, 31, 27 and 29. The groups are not literal square blocks.

The fixed regional criterion is $C=3s_P+1.5s_K+1.5s_D+c/d_{\max}$, where $s_P$, $s_K$ and $s_D$ are the standard deviations of regional population, cluster and county shares. Here $c$ averages within-region distances to regional centers and $d_{\max}$ is the maximum pairwise distance between the projected cluster coordinates. Table \ref{tab:nc-order} gives the regional ordering under the primary and alternative summaries, recorded before performance was evaluated.

## A5. Case Study Methods for Participation, Power and Model Sensitivity {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A5}{app:nc-ext}Here we give the methods behind @sec-nc-colleges and the sensitivity analyses of the case study, and at the end the Monte Carlo refinement and risk estimation of the main case-study run. Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext-results} gives their results. All numbers come from aggregate summaries of simulation runs, each of which recorded its parameters, code version and package versions. Unless stated otherwise, results use random volunteering, $\tau = 0$, $\kappa = 0.8$ and the corrected $t$ test, and they average the four planning years.

### Spatial-Model and Spillover-Form Sensitivity Analyses {.unnumbered .unlisted}

To check that the design comparison does not depend on the spatial model, we generated data at $N = 58$ with $\tau = 0$ from the spatial lag model and fit them with both a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model [@besag_spatial_1974; @cressie_statistics_1993] and the spatial lag model. In the reverse direction, we generated data from a CAR model with the same mean and fit them with both models. We also fit two Bayesian models to the spatial lag data, a CAR model with the prior of Leroux and colleagues [@leroux_estimation_2000; @lee_carbayes_2013] and a Bayesian spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009]. This section gives the four models, their priors, the Markov chain Monte Carlo settings and the convergence criterion. Finally, we replaced the proportional spillover exposure by a binary indicator of any treated neighbor and by a count of treated neighbors scaled by the mean number of neighbors, with the same form in the outcome model and the fit.

### From College-Level to Individual-Level Effects {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The trial outcome is a score measured on each trained professional and averaged within each college. We write a professional's score as a college effect plus individual variation, with total variance 1, which puts effects in individual standard-deviation units. The ICC is the share of that variance that lies between colleges, which makes the between-college variance equal to the ICC and the within-college variance equal to $1 - \text{ICC}$. Averaging the scores of $n_c$ professionals leaves the college part unchanged and divides the individual part by $n_c$. Therefore, the college mean has standard deviation $\sigma_c = \sqrt{\text{ICC} + (1 - \text{ICC})/n_c}$ [@donner_design_2000; @hayes_cluster_2017]. A college-level effect of $\beta$ standard deviations then corresponds to an individual-level standardized effect $d = \beta\sigma_c$. With $\tau = 0$, multiplying the effect and the noise by the same constant leaves $\hat\beta/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}$ unchanged, which means power for any $n_c$, ICC and $d$ follows from the simulated college-level results. Rerunning one setting with the effect and the noise both halved reproduced its estimates to within $6\times10^{-8}$. In a sensitivity analysis, the number of trained professionals grew with college population ($n_c$ averaging 25 over participants, ICC $= 0.05$), which made the noise variance differ between colleges. The fitted model stayed unweighted, as an analyst unaware of the difference would fit it.

### Estimation Models {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Every model in the sensitivity analysis has the mean $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \alpha \mathbf{1} + \beta \mathbf{Z} + \psi\,\text{Spill}$, where $\text{Spill} = \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z})$ is the proportional spillover covariate of the main analysis, and uses the 58-college queen geography. The spatial lag model of the main analysis is $\mathbf{Y} = \rho \mathbf{W} \mathbf{Y} + \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$, $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I})$. The CAR model is $\mathbf{Y} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{u} \sim N\{\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 (\mathbf{I} - \lambda \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sym}})^{-1}\}$, where $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is the symmetric matrix similar to the row-standardized $\mathbf{W}$ [@ord_estimation_1975]. We fit it by maximum likelihood with the `spautolm` function of the R package `spatialreg` [@bivand_r_2022]. For the reverse comparison, data were generated as $\mathbf{Y} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ with $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top = (\mathbf{I} - \rho \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{sym}})^{-1}$ and the same values of $\rho$ as the spatial lag data. These runs used four years, $\rho \in \{0, 0.2, 0.5\}$, $\psi \in \{0.5, 0.8\}$, both regimes and the nine designs, with 500 fits per setting.

The Bayesian CAR model [@leroux_estimation_2000] is $Y_j = \mu_j + \phi_j + e_j$, $e_j \sim N(0, \nu^2)$, with
\begin{equation*}
\phi_j \mid \phi_{-j} \sim N\left(\frac{\lambda \sum_k a_{jk}\phi_k}{\lambda \sum_k a_{jk} + 1 - \lambda},\; \frac{\sigma_\phi^2}{\lambda \sum_k a_{jk} + 1 - \lambda}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $a_{jk}$ is the binary queen adjacency. We used the defaults of the `S.CARleroux` function of the R package `CARBayes` [@lee_carbayes_2013], version 6.1.1: independent $N(0, 10^5)$ priors for the regression coefficients, inverse-gamma(1, 0.01) priors for $\nu^2$ and $\sigma_\phi^2$, and a uniform(0, 1) prior for $\lambda$. Each chain ran 25,000 iterations, discarding the first 5,000 and thinning by 5. At $\rho = 0.5$, where fewer than half the chains converged, we reran the same data with 100,000 iterations, discarding the first 20,000 and thinning by 20. The Bayesian spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009] has the same form as the maximum likelihood model, with the defaults of the `spBreg_lag` function of `spatialreg`, version 1.4.3: a $N(\mathbf{0}, 10^{12} \mathbf{I})$ prior for the regression coefficients, the prior $p(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2$, a Beta(1.01, 1.01) prior for $\rho$ rescaled to its feasible interval, and 10,000 draws of which the first 2,000 were discarded. Both Bayesian models used four years, $\rho \in \{0, 0.5\}$, $\psi = 0.8$, both regimes and the nine designs, with 100 fits per setting (14,400 fits per model), and both were fit to the same data as the maximum likelihood model. We report the posterior mean of $\beta$ and the 95\% equal-tailed credible interval. A chain was counted as converged when the effective sample size of $\beta$ was at least 400 and the absolute Geweke $z$ statistic [@geweke_evaluating_1992] was below 1.96.

### Monte Carlo Refinement and Risk Estimation in the Main Case-Study Run {.unnumbered .unlisted}

For randomized designs, the prespecified refinement schedule allowed $J = 100$, 200 or 400 and $R = 100$, 200, 400, 1,000, 2,000 or 4,000. Whichever source of Monte Carlo error, allocations or outcomes, contributed more to the shortfall from the precision targets was extended. All randomized designs met the targets at $J=100$ and $R=100$. For designs with a single possible assignment, only outcomes were extended. If an allocation occurs $n_a$ times among $J$ draws, its risk estimate enters the mean with weight $n_a/J$. Therefore, the variance due to outcome noise involves squared weights $(n_a/J)^2$, not $n_a/J^2$ as if duplicate estimates were independent. Bias and coverage use the same accounting of frequencies and covariances. The overall precision includes both variation across assignments and outcome noise given an assignment. A design whose sampled assignments happened to coincide is distinguished from one with only one possible assignment. Approximate Monte Carlo standard errors of setting-specific differences between designs treat the designs' random draws as independent, but averages across settings or models do not assume that shared allocations are independent. Settings with the same set of possible assignments shared their simulations, with annual treatment counts and population shares recalculated.

We report the estimated variance of risk both raw and with the contribution of outcome Monte Carlo noise subtracted. Signed corrected estimates are retained without truncation at zero. None is negative in the NC refinement. Quantiles and worst-decile means use noisy estimated conditional risks. To check for selection bias, worst-decile assignments were also identified with one half of the simulated outcomes and evaluated with the other half, and the roles of the two halves were then reversed. The cross-selected reductions relative to SRS were similar to or slightly larger than the reported ones. The Jaccard overlap of the two worst deciles describes sampled tail membership, not a confidence interval or population tail probability. For a design with only one possible assignment, an overlap of one is uninformative.

## A7. Pairwise Tests and Critical-Difference Diagrams {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A7}{app:supp-comparisons}Below are the test methods, the pairwise test results under queen contiguity and the critical-difference diagram behind results stated in the body of this chapter. The rook-contiguity results are in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}.

### Test Methods {.unnumbered .unlisted}

We compared designs within each neighbor type with a Friedman rank-sum test on scenario MSE [@friedman_use_1937], treating the 160 blocks as repeated measures across the six designs and SRS. SRS is the usual default for a cluster randomized trial, and it enters every test as a seventh member. Each design is compared with it as well as with the other designs. At $\beta = 1$ we followed the Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons [@nemenyi_distributionfree_1963; @demsar_statistical_2006] and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [@wilcoxon_individual_1945] with Holm's adjustment for multiple comparisons [@holm_simple_1979] for all 21 pairs. We repeated the Friedman test at each other value of $\beta$. Blocks within an incidence configuration share their surfaces, which means these tests treat dependent blocks as independent and overstate the information about variation from surface to surface. Therefore, we also ran paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with $t_{49}$ intervals for the mean difference, over 50 independent units, the 5 configurations times 10 surfaces. Each unit's MSE was averaged over that surface's blocks. These tests compared each pair of designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order, and each design with SRS within each spillover regime, with Holm's adjustment over the eight designs compared with SRS.

### Pairwise Tests Under Queen Contiguity {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Nemenyi comparisons (critical difference 0.712) separated 17 of the 21 pairs, and Incidence-Guided Saturation ranked better than SRS ($p = 0.011$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests separated 20 of the 21 pairs, all except Balanced Quartiles against SRS ($p = 0.15$). With SRS as a seventh member, the four pairs that Nemenyi comparisons did not separate were Balanced Quartiles against SRS ($p = 1.00$), $2\times2$ Blocking against High Incidence Focus ($p = 0.32$) and Checkerboard ($p = 0.39$), and Checkerboard against High Incidence Focus ($p = 1.00$). We also compared designs adjacent in the six-design mean-MSE order over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. Table \ref{tab:adjacent-pairs} gives the mean paired differences in MSE with $t_{49}$ 95\% intervals, and the Wilcoxon $p$-value was at most $4.9\times10^{-9}$ in every case. The better design of each pair had the lower MSE in all 50 units, except High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking, where it did so in 48 (96\%). This test follows the mean-MSE order, and it separated High Incidence Focus from $2\times2$ Blocking where the Nemenyi comparison of within-block ranks did not. It did so because each unit's MSE averages over both spillover regimes, and in that average the control-only losses of $2\times2$ Blocking outweigh its both-arms wins.

## A9. Rook Contiguity and the Bias--Variance Decomposition {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A9}{app:rook-figures}This section reports the results under rook contiguity and shows the decomposition of MSE into squared bias and variance for one incidence configuration under both neighbor types (Figure \ref{fig:biasvar}). Figure \ref{fig:mse-rook} gives the rook version of Figure \ref{fig:mse}, with the designs ordered for rook contiguity. Checkerboard under rook contiguity is flagged because $\beta$ is not identifiable (@sec-estimation).

Under rook contiguity at $\beta = 1$, pooled over the five incidence configurations, the mean-MSE order was Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.072), Balanced Quartiles (0.084), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.128), Isolation Buffer (0.133), High Incidence Focus (0.206), and Checkerboard (0.480) (Table \ref{tab:performance} and Figure \ref{fig:mse-rook}). The same order held within each of the five incidence configurations (Table \ref{tab:by-config}). Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest MSE in 97 of the 160 rook blocks (61\%), Balanced Quartiles in 60 (38\%), $2\times2$ Blocking in 2 and Isolation Buffer in 1. Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation's MSE was 0.045 under both-arms spillover and 0.098 under control-only spillover, against 0.042 and 0.125 for Balanced Quartiles. Coverage was between 0.948 and 0.952 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was 0.162 (Table \ref{tab:performance}). Within single incidence configurations, rook coverage was between 0.944 and 0.954 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was between 0.155 and 0.165.

With SRS as a seventh member, the Friedman test rejected equal ranks ($\chi^2 = 795.77$, $\text{df} = 6$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests separated every pair except two: Balanced Quartiles against SRS, and $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer, which were close and swapped order at some values of $\beta$ ($2\times2$ Blocking had the lower MSE in 36 of the 50 independent units, and Isolation Buffer the slightly better average rank, 4.21 against 4.33). Nemenyi comparisons separated 17 of the 21 pairs. They left Incidence-Guided Saturation, Balanced Quartiles and SRS unseparated from one another, and $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer unseparated from each other ($p = 1.00$). Incidence-Guided Saturation nevertheless had the lower MSE in 48 of the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units against Balanced Quartiles (test methods in Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons}), and its paired comparisons with SRS within each regime appear in @sec-vs-srs.

Checkerboard under rook contiguity is a different case: $\beta$ is not identifiable, and the coefficient on $\mathbf{Z}$ estimates $\beta - \psi$ (@sec-estimation). At $\beta = 1$, Checkerboard's mean bias was $-0.502$, $-0.600$, $-0.704$, and $-0.802$ at $\psi = 0.5$, 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8, while its mean standard deviation stayed between 0.201 and 0.208. Squared bias, averaged over scenarios, accounted for 0.438 of its MSE of 0.480 (Figure \ref{fig:biasvar-rook}). Its coverage fell from 0.337 at $\psi = 0.5$ to 0.031 at $\psi = 0.8$, and was between 0.146 and 0.171 at every level of $\rho$, against 0.949 to 0.952 under queen contiguity (Table \ref{tab:checkerboard-coverage} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables}). With $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}$, the two spillover regimes define the same outcome model. The observed MSEs, 0.477 under the both-arms regime and 0.483 under the control-only regime, differ only by Monte Carlo error. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard's estimates were precise but centered on $\beta - \psi$ rather than $\beta$. Under queen contiguity they were centered on $\beta$ but imprecise. We keep these estimates in every ranking and flag them.

## A10. Sensitivity Analysis Without the Spillover Term {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A10}{app:oracle-nonoracle}The non-oracle model, which omits the spillover term, was biased for every design. Table \ref{tab:oracle-nonoracle} gives both models' MSE, bias, and coverage for each design. At $\beta = 1$, and setting aside Checkerboard under rook contiguity, its bias ranged from $-0.121$ to $-0.400$ and its coverage from 0.536 to 0.907 across designs and neighbor types. For Checkerboard under rook contiguity, the two models coincide: once the aliased spillover column is dropped, the oracle model is the non-oracle model. Omitting the spillover term also removes a column that can be nearly collinear with $\mathbf{Z}$, and the non-oracle estimates were accordingly less variable for some designs. Under queen contiguity, the non-oracle MSE was lower than the oracle MSE for every design, most of all for Checkerboard (oracle 1.087, non-oracle 0.108) and $2\times2$ Blocking (oracle 0.319, non-oracle 0.121). Under rook contiguity it was higher for every design except $2\times2$ Blocking (0.128 under both models) and Checkerboard (identical). However, where a design's non-oracle MSE was lower, its estimate was biased and its intervals under-covered, which means the lower MSE does not support valid inference. These results do not change the recommendation: Incidence-Guided Saturation also had the lowest non-oracle MSE under both neighbor types (0.087 under queen contiguity and 0.086 under rook contiguity).

## A11. Additional Case Study Results {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A11}{app:nc-results}**Run sizes.** The main run generated 7,598,000 independent outcome fits. Every setting was complete and met its prespecified precision targets for mean MSE and coverage. ## A12. Case Study Participation, Power and Sensitivity Results {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\applabel{A12}{app:nc-ext-results}This section gives the results of the analyses described in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}. Unless stated otherwise, results use random volunteering, $\tau = 0$, $\kappa = 0.8$ and the corrected $t$ test, and they average the four planning years.

### Colleges Needed and Smallest Detectable Effect {.unnumbered .unlisted}

With $n_c = 25$ and an ICC of 0.05, values chosen for illustration rather than estimated for this trial, $\sigma_c = 0.30$. Table \ref{tab:nc-translation} gives the results for other values. Under both-arms spillover, an individual-level effect of $d = 0.3$ then gives power 0.71 to 0.72 with 29 colleges and 0.96 with 58, for SRS and for both saturation designs. Under control-only spillover the same effect gives power 0.49 with 29 colleges and 0.53 with 58 under SRS, and 0.51 with 29 colleges and 0.64 with 58 under Incidence-Guided Saturation (Table \ref{tab:nc-translation}).

Table \ref{tab:nc-power} gives, for each design, the number of colleges needed for 80\% power and the smallest college-level effect detectable with 80\% power at 29 and 58 colleges. Table \ref{tab:nc-translation} gives the power of the corrected $t$ test with simple random sampling for an individual-level standardized effect $d$. The number of colleges needed is interpolated monotonically between the simulated values of $N$ within each year, averaged over years and rounded up to a whole college. Results at $\rho = 0$ differed from those at $\rho = 0.5$ by about two colleges or fewer. Power curves are not always monotone in $N$: some drops in power between successive values of $N$ are larger than Monte Carlo error, because the participant subsets differ between values of $N$. We report the dips rather than smooth them.

### Interval Calibration {.unnumbered .unlisted}

We tried several corrections and adopted a method only if its coverage lay between 0.9400 and 0.9600 for every design and regime. On the stored fits of the main case study ($\tau = 0$), the Wald interval covered 0.9260 to 0.9360 by design and regime. A $t$ reference distribution alone gave 0.9320 to 0.9410, a degrees-of-freedom-corrected standard error alone 0.9350 to 0.9440, and the two together 0.9410 to 0.9490. In a separate run of 500 fits per setting at 58 colleges, parametric percentile bootstrap intervals with 499 replicates covered 0.9010 to 0.9360, parametric bootstrap-$t$ intervals 0.9320 to 0.9580 and profile-likelihood intervals 0.9180 to 0.9470. Only the $t$ interval with the corrected standard error met the rule on the stored fits. In the separate 500-fit run it covered 0.9280 to 0.9580 and narrowly missed the rule there, which every other method also missed. The method was chosen on the stored fits of the main case study. The participation runs are new simulations that played no part in that choice, and Table \ref{tab:nc-calibration} shows the interval's size and coverage in them at each number of participating colleges. Table \ref{tab:interval-comparison} compares the Wald and corrected intervals for each design in the grid study and the main case study.

### Guidance Under Partial Participation {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Table \ref{tab:nc-guidance} gives each design's mean MSE relative to SRS at $\beta = 1$ for 20, 29, 40 and 58 participating colleges. When colleges with higher incidence were more likely to volunteer, the ratios at 20 and 29 colleges were within 0.02 of 1 for both saturation designs and Balanced Quartiles under either regime, and within 0.03 for Balanced Halves. Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer remained the worst designs. The four saturation regions were rebuilt on the participants with at least two colleges required in every region. Before that requirement was imposed, a region with fewer than two colleges occurred in 1 of the 50 random subsets at 15 colleges and in one incidence-weighted subset at 20 colleges. Imposing it changed the regions of only two distinct participant subsets and changed no ratio in Table \ref{tab:nc-guidance} by more than 0.01.

### Share of Incidence in Treated Colleges {.unnumbered .unlisted}

With all 58 colleges, Incidence-Guided Saturation's mean share of the summed college incidence rates in treated colleges was 51.1\%, against 50.4\% for Saturation Quadrants, 50.0\% for SRS and 62.2\% for High Incidence Focus. Its mean share of deaths was 49.2\%, against 49.6\%, 49.7\% and 35.4\%. On the grid, the gain of Incidence-Guided Saturation over Saturation Quadrants in treated incidence share averaged 2.1 to 3.1 percentage points across the five incidence configurations, while the treated incidence share of High Incidence Focus itself reached 0.75 to 0.77 because it treats the highest-incidence clusters without randomization. Grid clusters have equal populations, which makes rate share and death share coincide there. The gain rose almost linearly with the spread of the regions' mean incidence ranks, and the NC regions lie at the low end of that spread.

### Formal Tests for the Case Study {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Friedman tests over the 24 combinations of year, $\rho$ and $\psi$ rejected equal ranks of the nine designs in all four combinations of regime and $\tau$ ($\chi^2 = 135.3$, 153.8, 150.7 and 179.8 on 8 degrees of freedom, $p \le 2.3\times10^{-25}$, and Nemenyi critical difference 2.45). Under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants and Incidence-Guided Saturation had the two best average ranks (1.67 and 1.79 with $\tau = 0$, and 1.29 and 1.71 with $\tau = 1$), and SRS ranked seventh with $\tau = 0$ and sixth with $\tau = 1$. Under both-arms spillover with $\tau = 0$, High Incidence Focus ranked first (1.88) and SRS sixth (5.17), with the balancing and saturation designs between them. These tests treat the 24 blocks as independent, although the years share one map and some designs share their simulations across years. Therefore, they describe the consistency of the ordering rather than independent evidence.

### Unequal Numbers of Trained Professionals {.unnumbered .unlisted}

With $n_c$ proportional to college population and averaging 25, and ICC $= 0.05$, power fell by 0.097 on average across designs, settings and effect sizes. For $d = 0.3$ under both-arms spillover, the mean power over the nine designs fell from 0.59 to 0.46 with 20 colleges and from 0.88 to 0.77 with 58. MSE rose by a factor of 1.24 to 1.84 across designs and settings, and no design gained relative to the others.

With the longer chains, 83.1\% of the Bayesian CAR chains at $\rho = 0.5$ converged, against 46.2\% for the shorter chains, but 12.5\% still had an absolute Geweke $z$ of at least 1.96, against about 5\% expected by chance. Among converged chains, the Bayesian CAR estimate was biased by $+0.138$ under both-arms spillover and $+0.219$ under control-only spillover, with credible-interval coverage of 0.904 and 0.877. For maximum likelihood on the same data, the biases were $+0.023$ and $+0.028$ and the corrected $t$ coverage 0.950 and 0.946. Of the Bayesian spatial lag chains, 94.9\% converged. The median effective sample size of $\beta$ was 8,000 (minimum 5,897), and 5.1\% of chains had an absolute Geweke $z$ of at least 1.96. The model's posterior means correlated 0.999 with the maximum likelihood estimates (mean absolute difference 0.017). Its bias was at most 0.039 in absolute value in every combination of $\rho$ and regime, and its credible intervals covered 0.946 to 0.953 over all chains (0.945 to 0.953 over converged chains). The Spearman correlation of its design ordering with that of maximum likelihood averaged 0.96 to 1.00 across the four combinations of $\rho$ and regime (0.83 in the lowest single block), and the best design agreed in every block. In the maximum likelihood comparison of the spatial lag and CAR models, the saturation designs' MSE under control-only spillover was 0.76 to 0.82 times that of SRS in every combination of generating model and fitted model. When the CAR model was fit to spatial lag data, its estimates were biased by 0.035 and 0.085 at $\rho = 0.2$ and by 0.110 and 0.205 at $\rho = 0.5$ under both-arms and control-only spillover. When it was fit to CAR data, its bias was at most 0.005.

### Form of the Spillover Exposure {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Under the binary form, $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathbb{I}\{\text{any treated queen neighbor}\}$, multiplied by $\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{Z}$ under control-only spillover. Under the count form, $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) = (1/\bar d) \times$ (number of treated queen neighbors), where $\bar d = 4.93$ is the mean number of queen neighbors. A college of average degree with every neighbor treated has $\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{Z}) = 1$ and receives $\psi$, as under the proportional form. Table \ref{tab:nc-forms} compares the three forms. With the binary form, Isolation Buffer is never identifiable, because every control has a treated neighbor, and under control-only spillover no design was identifiable in every fit. The saturation designs were identifiable most often there (in 89.7\% and 91.7\% of fits) and, among identifiable fits, had MSE 0.70 to 0.71 times that of SRS.
